utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It's good to see such smiling and familiar faces. We are now to commence final submissions. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please Your Honours, I will start our closing with the words of one of the victims in this case, Witness L-06, about a particular moment at Lapusnik. He said: "This Fatmir Limaj came and asked us, he said, You, you, why are you here for? Then he asked me and I said, I don't know. I went to look for my cousin, and they brought me here. I don't know why. He," meaning Fatmir Limaj, "said, If you have something - if you have done something, you will be killed. If you are innocent, you will go home." These words capture much of what was Lapusnik in the summer of 1998. It was an arbitrary place, where men were brought on the flimsiest of suspicions, accused of collaboration for no good reason at all or were brought simply because they were Serb men. Recall the testimony of Ramadan Behluli, who even now in this courtroom, accused two men who became victims in Lapusnik of collaboration based on nothing, we submit, nothing at all. Recall the testimony of Ivan and Vojko Bakrac, who described how KLA soldiers boarded their bus in Carraleve and took off all the Serb men. The four men who were taken off the bus ended up in Lapusnik. Two of them were murdered, and two survived -- the only Serbs who survived Lapusnik. Lapusnik was also a place where the prisoners were kept in the dark, both in the literal sense, in their cramped, hot, repulsive little prison rooms, and in the figurative sense in that they were never told why they were being detained and never afforded even the most basic protection and procedures to determine if there was any basis - any basis at all - for their arrest and detention, procedures that we say are the right of every human being in a war. Lapusnik was also a violent and frightening place, where men sat day after day, crushed together, many barely conscious, close to death, not knowing what the next day would bring, and regularly pulled from their rooms to be severely beaten, humiliated, tortured, and in many cases murdered. And finally, Your Honours, Lapusnik was a place that was under the command of Fatmir Limaj. Fatmir Limaj came to the prison, and the prisoners saw - they saw - that this Commander Celiku was in charge. He exercised his authority in the prison on several occasions arbitrarily, imperiously, ordered some of the prisoners released. No substitute, we say, for the proper procedures required by the law. He knew what was happening in that prison; it was under his command. He knew it was wrong, and for that reason the prisoners who were ordered released were also required to promise that they would never speak about the prison or they were required to say that they had been treated properly there. Your Honours, at the beginning of this trial, Mr. Cayley said that: "The essential facts of this case are as straightforward as they are compelling." The evidence has shown just that. The Prosecution submits that the three accused who sit here before you today are guilty, guilty of the crimes that are charged against them in the indictment. The facts have shown, Your Honours, that in May, June, and July of 1998, the Celiku 3 unit was in charge of the area below -- in Lapusnik below the Peja-Prishtine highway, meaning to the south of that road. At its peak, the Celiku 3 unit had well over 70 soldiers and it controlled five fighting positions which looked out over the valley towards the Serbian forces. These fighting positions constituted a KLA front line, protecting a large area under KLA control. From these fighting positions, KLA soldiers also controlled and monitored a KLA roadblock on the Peja-Pristina highway and monitored Serbian forces in Komorane. In the area of Lapusnik controlled by the Celiku 3 unit, in addition to the roadblock and the five fighting positions, there was a headquarters, a medical clinic, a kitchen where the soldiers gathered to eat, and a prison. A prison. At this time, in the summer of 1998 and before, the KLA had, as Mr. Limaj himself has admitted, an express policy targeting Albanians suspected of collaboration. Only no definition was ever provided of what it meant to be a collaborator, and no procedures were ever implemented to investigate or to evaluate allegations of collaboration. As a result, Albanian men who posed no threat, in our submission, to the KLA were arrested and detained. They were arrested for no good reason at all, often because of their mere association with Serbs. No proper procedures were followed, and none of these men were ever given an opportunity to defend themselves. At the same time, it is submitted that the KLA targeted Serb men who were civilians, arresting them at roadblocks, pulling them from buses and cars, and detaining them. This is not to say by any means that these were the primary objectives of the KLA or that the KLA did not have other noble objectives, and it is not to say that all of the members by any means of the KLA were involved in these activities; it is, however, the fact that the targeting of Albanians suspected of collaboration and the targeting of Serb civilian men were indeed features of KLA policy during the summer of 1998. In the area under Fatmir Limaj's control, all of the Albanian and Serb men who were arrested were brought to Lapusnik, where they were detained in a prison in abhorrent conditions which would have been criminal even if the detentions had somehow been justified. The prisoners in Lapusnik were interrogated, beaten, tortured, and in many cases murdered. At the end of July 1998, when the Celiku 3 unit lost control of Lapusnik, the remaining Albanian prisoners - for there were no Serb survivors at this point - were marched into the mountains where half were released and half were murdered. The evidence has shown that the three accused who sit here today played essential roles in the Lapusnik prison. Haradin Bala was a guard in the prison in Lapusnik. He guarded the gates of the compound, locked and unlocked doors, brought food from the kitchen across the road to the prisoners as well as water and cigarettes, and he moved the prisoners around the compound. On a number of occasions he participated in brutal and severe beatings of prisoners and in their murders. He forced prisoners to bury the bodies of other prisoners who had been murdered. When the prison was overrun, Haradin Bala and another guard marched the remaining prisoners into the Berisa Mountains. He met up with Fatmir Limaj along the way and received instructions and a third soldier. He then continued the march and released some of the prisoners. Then he ordered the remaining prisoners to line up and he said: "This is your death sentence." "This is your death sentence." These words from Haradin Bala are the last words that ten of the men in the line ever heard on this earth. After they were spoken, Haradin Bala and two other soldiers fired on the prisoners, killing ten of them. Isak Musliu was the commander of Celiku 3. From the beginning of June he was based at a headquarters located near the clinic, a mere 2 to 300 metres away from the prison. He commanded over the fighting positions and over the soldiers who were in charge of each of the fighting positions. Musliu commanded the soldiers during the 29th of May fighting. He was consulted about important matters that arose, for example, at the roadblock. When the United States Ambassador Christopher Hill came to the roadblock at the end of June, it was Isak Musliu who spoke with him for over an hour. Musliu admitted new soldiers into Celiku 3 and he gave permission to soldiers to travel to other areas. He disciplined soldiers. When the medical clinic needed supplies, Dr. Gashi would go to Isak Musliu, and Musliu would arrange for the supplies to be brought. Musliu was also in charge of the prison. He gave orders to guards there. He was present in the prison, and on numerous occasions he participated in brutal beatings, torture, and murder within the prison, frequently wearing a mask, not to protect himself -- not to protect his identity from the Serb forces, which is why most people in the KLA wore masks, but in an extraordinary act of cowardice to try to protect his identity from his victims. Fatmir Limaj was the commander of a larger area around Klecke that included Lapusnik. Celiku 1 was based in Klecke and existed from March or April of 1998. When the KLA seized control of Lapusnik on the 9th of May, 1998, it soon became Celiku 3 under Limaj's command. Limaj installed Isak Musliu as the commander of Celiku 3 and told the soldiers that they should go through Isak Musliu for anything they needed and that he, Limaj, was in charge of the larger area. During May, June, and July of 1998, Limaj came to Lapusnik approximately 20 times, which is nearly twice a week. He participated in all the major battles in Lapusnik and was the commander of the soldiers during the 9th of May and the 29th of May fighting. In June and later in September, it was Fatmir Limaj who spoke to the media about the KLA's successes in Lapusnik. He made decisions about the disciplining of soldiers and about who would be in charge of the fighting positions in Lapusnik. He conducted the oath ceremony in Lapusnik and he came with Byslym Zyrapi to Lapusnik to bring a new gun to the front line. He went to the headquarters in Lapusnik and to the kitchen, and he met with Isak Musliu in Lapusnik. He checked on the clinic to see if it was operating properly and if it needed anything. He was in command of the prison, and on several occasions he made decisions about who would be released from the prison. On at least one occasion, he personally insisted that before a prisoner could be released he would have to make a statement swearing not to talk about what happened there at Lapusnik. At the end of July when the prisoners were marched into Berisa, Limaj was consulted about what should happen to them and thereafter half of the prisoners were released and half were murdered. These are the facts, Your Honours, straightforward and compelling. The accused are guilty for directly committing some of the crimes charged in the indictment and for planning or ordering others. They are guilty for participating in a joint criminal enterprise, whether this joint criminal enterprise is conceived as a common plan or as a system of ill-treatment. The purpose of the common plan or system of ill-treatment was to target Albanians suspected of collaboration and Serb civilians for detention, violence, and murder. The crimes charged were either within the scope of the joint criminal enterprise or were clearly foreseeable to the accused. Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu are also responsible for failing to prevent or punish the crimes charged in the indictment. In its final brief, submitted on the 20th of July of this year, the Prosecution presented in extensive detail its analysis of the evidence and of the law in this case. It is not our intention, you will be relieved to know, to repeat everything that has been set out in that brief. Rather, the Prosecution will use these oral submissions to focus on particular points that are in dispute and to respond to some, though not all, of the arguments made by the Defence in its final brief. I will start by addressing the roles of the accused. Mr. Black will then address the crimes, and Mr. Nicholls will address the issues of armed conflict and widespread and systematic attack. I will then finish by addressing the issue of sentencing. A few preliminary words about the arguments that have been made by the Defence. In the respectful submission of the Prosecution, the final brief of the Defence is simply replete with errors of fact and analysis. It will not be possible in these closings for the Prosecution to identify all of the errors, though we will identify some. The errors fall into several broad categories. First, the Defence brief cites to numerous documents and statements that are simply not in evidence, and the Prosecution moves to strike these matters from the Defence final brief. Specifically, footnotes 1 through 11, 13 to 14, 16 to 23, 25, 28, 259, 470, 958, 1.063, 1.074, 1120, 1184; and paragraph 768, 788, and 795 cite to evidence that is simply not in the record and therefore, in our submission, is not properly part of a final brief. Second, the Defence has sought in its final brief to relitigate numerous issues that were briefed, argued, and decided during trial. In the submission of the Prosecution, these issues have been settled and their reconsideration are not properly the subject of a final brief. Third, the Defence brief asserts a number of facts that are simply not supported by the record. For example, in paragraph 619 the Defence asserts that there were many soldiers in the KLA that chose the pseudonym Shala. The claim is not footnoted, and that's no surprise because there is no evidence whatsoever to support this claim in the record. In this, Sylejman Selimi was asked in cross-examination on page 2204 of the transcript if he knew of any soldiers with the pseudonym of Shala, and he responded "no." Fourth, on numerous occasions the Defence misstates the record, sometimes getting the evidence exactly wrong. For example, in paragraphs 522 and 524, the Defence says that none of the kidnappings in this case occurred in the area that later became the 121 Brigade; that's simply not correct. If you look at Exhibit DL7, which is now being shown on the Sanction, the map on which Fatmir Limaj drew what he says was the area of the 121 Brigade in green and the description of this area that he provides at pages 5966 to 67 of the record, it is clear that this area includes Kroimire, where Hetem Rexhaj was kidnapped; Petrastica, where Witness L-7 was kidnapped; Lapusnik, where Shaban Hoti, L-01, and Miroslav Suljnic were kidnapped; and Carraleve, Carraleve, where numerous Serb and Albanian victims in this case were kidnapped. Fifth, the Defence often makes factual assertions which are extremely misleading. For example, in paragraph 166, the Defence states that: "Witness Ivan Bakrac testified that Genov was beaten with automatic rifles, sharp objects, et cetera, but failed to mention this in his statement to the investigator." Well, in fact, the witness did discuss the beating of Genov in his statement to the investigator; the only thing he did not talk about in his prior statement was the precise weapons used in the beating. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I will not belabour these points with further examples, though there are many, and other examples will be addressed at other points in the closing. I have no doubt that the Chamber will scrutinise carefully all of the legal and factual assertions made by both sides in this case, in both the written filings already submitted and the oral submissions made this week. In the submission of the Prosecution, the evidence establishes beyond all possible doubt that there was in fact a prison, a KLA prison, in Lapusnik and that the prisoners there were subjected to criminal abuse, torture, and murder. It is noteworthy that while the Defence challenged some of the initial victims who testified on whether the camp was in Lapusnik, it eventually gave up on this line of questioning. In the final brief of the Defence, we submit that there is no real challenge to the substantial evidence that the prison was in fact in Lapusnik. After I finish, Mr. Black will address the crimes that occurred in Lapusnik. The question that I will address is the role and responsibility of the three accused for these crimes, beginning with Fatmir Limaj. The Prosecution submits that multiple and independent sources of evidence show that Fatmir Limaj was in fact the commander of a larger area around Klecke, including Lapusnik, and that he was the overall commander of the prison in Lapusnik. There are two groups of witnesses who testify about Limaj's role in Lapusnik: Victims who were inside of the prison walls of Lapusnik and who saw Limaj within the prison and KLA soldiers, and others who were on the outside of the prison and who testify about his command role over Lapusnik. Let's begin with those outside of the prison. Ramiz Qeriqi testified that the area he drew on Prosecution Exhibit 154, which is now up on the Sanction, including Lapusnik, was under the command of Klecke, meaning Fatmir Limaj, from May of 1998 onwards. Qeriqi also provide -- provided detailed information about how the unit in Kroimire was organised and how soldiers under Qeriqi's command took orders from him at this time. The Defence contends in paragraph 531 of their brief that there is no evidence that Qeriqi, Luan, was a subordinate of Limaj; that's not true. Qeriqi himself testified that the chain of command ran from Likovc to Klecke, meaning Fatmir Limaj, to Kroimire. Qeriqi said: "From Klecke, every instruction came from Fatmir Limaj." The Defence further contends that the Prosecution credits Ramiz Qeriqi's denial of his own involvement in the criminal activity, but that is simply false. It is frequently the case that witnesses will tell the truth about certain matters but not about others, and will in particular minimise their own role in criminal activity. It would be wrong, we submit, simply to throw out Qeriqi's testimony because it was found, if it was found, that he did not admit to his own culpability in events. The question rather is whether the testimony of Qeriqi about Limaj's command role is corroborated by other evidence, and in fact it is. Ramadan Behluli stated in his interview with the OTP, which is in evidence as Exhibit P121, that by the spring of 1998, Limaj was the commander of the zone in which Kroimire was located. Behluli drew Prosecution Exhibit 119, which is now on the Sanction, which matches the drawing of Qeriqi, and which he described to be the area including Lapusnik under Klecka's control by July 1998. Behluli also corroborated Qeriqi's evidence about how the unit in Kroimire functioned and how he received orders. He also described how Fatmir Limaj came to Kroimire in June of 1998 on the 17th after fighting broke out there and instructed Behluli to attack Serbian fighters without waiting for further orders. In Shukri Buja's OTP interview, Prosecution Exhibit 160, he corroborated both Ramiz Qeriqi and Ramadan Behluli concerning Limaj's role. He explained in detail how Limaj came to be in a command position in Klecke, first over the areas being organised by Qeriqi and Shukri Buja and later over other villages, including Lapusnik and Luznica. Shukri Buja, not the OTP, was the first in the interview to describe Limaj as a commander, stating at page 23 that: "I have always counted him, Fatmir Limaj, as my first commander on this basis." He went on to describe Limaj at another point in the interview as the coordinator of the area around Klecke, but Buja made it clear that Limaj told him what to do. Buja said: "I asked Limaj what we should do." And at another point he said when talking about arrested persons that: "He received instructions there," meaning Klecke, "from Commander Celiku." Buja, for his part, drew Prosecution Exhibit 159, which is up on the Sanction, a diagram of the villages under Limaj's control which included Kroimire, Klecke, and Lapusnik. This diagram corroborates the maps drawn by Qeriqi and Behluli. So what weight should be given to the OTP interviews, which are in evidence, of Ramadan Behluli and Shukri Buja, particularly in light of their testimony in court? For its part, the Defence attempts to revisit this Chamber's decisions declaring both of these witnesses hostile and its decision to admit into evidence, for the truth of the matter, the OTP interviews of these witnesses. These issues were already decided, however, by the Chamber. And so the Defence then proposes, starting at paragraph 79, a series of so-called guiding principles to evaluate the prior interviews of these witnesses. Well, it turns out that these so-called guiding principles are simply a rehash of the same arguments against admitting the statements in the first place, and application of the principles proposed by the Defence would necessarily preclude automatically any reliance whatsoever on the prior statements. The question for the Chamber, in this submission of the Prosecution, is really more simple: On each matter about which Behluli and Buja testified, did they tell the truth in their prior statements or did they tell the truth in court? The Prosecution submits that when all of the circumstances of the prior interviews are considered, along with all of the other evidence in the case, it is clear that with regard to Limaj's command during May, June, and July of 1998, Behluli and Buja were truthful in their prior interviews and were not truthful in court. How otherwise to explain their prior interviews? Could they have been mistaken? No. Both witnesses were very specific and clear about their testimony in the OTP interviews, and it is impossible to believe that they both managed to make the same mistakes about Limaj's command. Did they have reason to lie or exaggerate in their prior interviews? No. Neither witness had a reason to lie about Fatmir Limaj's command, and both witnesses were careful in their answers in the OTP interview. There is no evidence that they exaggerated. The Defence proposes another explanation: That the OTP led these witnesses into their answers; the record, however, proves otherwise. The Chamber has the video record of the Behluli and Buja interviews. It can review their entire interviews from beginning to end and decide for itself. It should be clear that the evidence about Limaj's command came from the witnesses, that the witnesses provided the information voluntarily, and that they carefully qualified their answers and their knowledge. I will not play the interviews now, but I will note a few examples. Ramadan Behluli, at page 21 of his interview, was the first one in the interview even to mention the name "Fatmir Limaj," describing him as the commander of the zone. With respect to Shukri Buja, the Defence contends in paragraph 97 of their brief that the diagram drawn by Shukri Buja, Exhibit 159 which was shown a few moments ago, was dictated by the interviewer. Watch the interview, starting at page 37 of the transcript. Buja by this point in the interview has already described the structure in Kroimire and then he is asked if there are other points like Kroimire that are under the command of Klecke. When he says that there are, he is asked to draw the points under Klecka's command on a diagram. He then draws Kroimire, Petrastica, Luznica, Lapusnik, and others. The only uncertainty he expresses is whether the specific points came into being in May or in June, because the question that is put to him is to draw the points that existed in May. After he draws the diagram he says: "This was approximately the organisation." The diagram was not dictated to the witness; he drew it himself and he provided all of the information in it. The Defence also suggests that Buja had to be asked several times to confirm the structure in Kroimire. Again, look at the interview; it's at page 36. The witness is simply being asked to confirm information about the structure that he has already provided, and he is asked the question several times simply to focus him on the question being asked. Once focussed on the question, he confirmed without difficulty Limaj's command over Kroimire. One additional point raised by the Defence regarding Shukri Buja. In its continual effort to shift the focus on to the Prosecution and put the Prosecution on trial in this case, a tactic that we expect to be repeated in the closing submissions of the Defence, the Defence has suggested in paragraph 150 that the Prosecution has taken contrary positions with respect to Shukri Buja: That he testified in the Milosevic case about the same matters that he testified about in court in this case and was not treated as a hostile witness. Well, this is simply false. As Shukri Buja himself stated in court, he testified in Milosevic about events that occurred in Racak in 1999, a completely different subject. Likewise, the Prosecution has not taken conflicting positions on Dragan Jasovic. In this case, the Prosecution has taken the position that in light of the substantial evidence against Mr. Jasovic that has been admitted into evidence in this case, the Trial Chamber should rely on the testimony of Jasovic, if at all, only on very narrow matters for which there exists substantial corroboration. This position is entirely consistent with the Prosecution's position in Milosevic. The evidence provided by Ramiz Qeriqi, Shukri Buja, and Ramadan Behluli concerning Fatmir Limaj's command during the summer of 1998 is further corroborated by the testimony of Witness L-64, who testified that Limaj was the overall commander over Lapusnik after the 9th of May battle, and who provided specific evidence of the exercise of Limaj's command in Lapusnik. Witness L-64 also drew a diagram of the area under Klecka's command, Exhibit 173 which is up on the Sanction, which included Lapusnik and which is entirely consistent with the maps and diagrams of the other witnesses. The Defence argues that L-64 was induced to give his testimony in exchange for having charges against him dismissed. This argument, however, is rife with inaccurate and misleading assertions. In paragraph 125, they suggest that L-64 was summonsed by the OTP as a suspect and that two months later his status had changed to that of a witness. Well in fact, he was informed he was being interviewed as a witness before the start of the very first interview with the OTP in May 2003. In paragraph 126, the Defence asserts that L-64 was sitting in jail when he was summonsed by the OTP; this is of course not true. L-64 gave interviews to the OTP in May and June of 2003 before there were any charges against him. And before there were any charges against him, before there could be even a suggestion of an inducement to fabricate anything, L-64 told the OTP in recorded interviews that Limaj was the commander of a larger area, including Lapusnik, in the summer of 1998, that he appointed Isak Musliu to be the commander in Lapusnik, that Musliu was the commander of the soldiers in Lapusnik, that there was a prison in Lapusnik where prisoners were kept in repulsive conditions, and that Haradin Bala was a guard in the prison. The Defence further asserts repeatedly in paragraphs 138, 284, 1.026 that L-64 said in his testimony that he did not know anything about the structure of the KLA; well of course this is not at all what he said. He said only that he did not have knowledge of the command of different zones of the KLA in Kosovo. He quite plainly and consistently stated that he knew the command structure in Lapusnik and that he knew the other areas under Limaj's command. At the end of the day the question is whether, even if the Trial Chamber finds that Witness L-64 was not entirely forthcoming with regard to certain matters regarding himself including his drug history, it can nonetheless rely upon his evidence with regard to events in Lapusnik. Although Witness L-64 was the only former KLA member who was willing to come into this courtroom to testify both to the structure of the KLA in Lapusnik and to the existence of the prison there, virtually all of his evidence on both of these issues is corroborated by other evidence. And that, Your Honours, is fully laid out in our final brief. It defies credibility that L-64 could concoct such a story that matches up with so many other independent pieces of evidence. In addition to these witnesses, there is other evidence which is set forth in our final brief that corroborates the evidence of Limaj's command in Lapusnik and the prison there, including the testimony of Witness L-95, who testified that at the time of the fall of Lapusnik in July of 1998, he understood Limaj, based in Klecke, to be in charge of an area that extended up to the Peja-Pristina road, including Lapusnik. And Witness L-96, who testified that while searching for someone who had been kidnapped by the KLA in July of 1998, he learned that Limaj was the commander of the region. This is the evidence of Limaj's command from outside of the prison. What about the the evidence from inside the prison? Virtually all of the victims - L-04, L-06, L-07, L-10, Ivan Bakrac, and by description, we submit, Vojko Bakrac - saw Limaj inside of the prison and observed him to the the commander there. Their descriptions of Limaj and their descriptions of his role are remarkably consistent. In addition, Witness L-96 saw Limaj during the march to Berisa and heard Haradin Bala say that he would ask Commander Celiku what he should do with the prisoners. Remember, these prisoners only saw what they could inside the walls of the prison and as they were leaving Lapusnik. They could not have known what was happening outside of the prison walls in Lapusnik or in the area surrounding Lapusnik. They could not have known in detail the structure of the KLA in the area, and they certainly could not have known that Limaj came to Lapusnik nearly twice a week during June and July of 1998. The fact that the evidence of the prisoners inside the prison is consistent with the evidence from the witnesses outside the prison is powerful evidence of Limaj's role. In the face of this evidence, the Defence suggests that the victims simply added - simply added - Limaj to their accounts. Well, was this done unintentionally by all of the different victims? If so, it is remarkable, impossible we would say, that all of these various victims could have unconsciously made up the same story. Was it done intentionally? If so, why? The victims are not out to get Fatmir Limaj, and some even credited him for the fact that they survived the prison. Why would they make that up? Also, it is remarkable that if the victims -- that the victims could have concocted a story, consciously or unconsciously, that so matches up with the witnesses from outside the prison. No, these victims did not make up Limaj's command of the prisons -- prison. Look at Exhibit P53. It is a document that purports to be an interview with Hisni Murseli given to the Serb authorities in January 1999. The evidence is that this report has been in the possession of the OTP since June of 1999, long before any of the victims in this case were interviewed. The report describes how in the summer of 1998 Fatmir Limaj was the commander of various villages, including Lapusnik, and that there was a prison in Lapusnik where Serbs and Albanians were held. Under the circumstances, it is impossible to know for sure whether the information in this report came from Hisni Murseli or from the Serbian authorities who interviewed Hisni Murseli, though it should be said that much of what is said in the report has been corroborated by other witnesses. The issue, however, at the moment is not where the information came from. The point is that if the Defence argument is to be believed, then whoever provided the information for this report before June of 1999 must also be part of this unconscious or conscious conspiracy hatched years later, according to the Defence, to tie Limaj with the prison in Lapusnik. And what about Exhibits P23 [sic] and P24 [sic], which purport to be Serbian interviews of witnesses L-04 and L-06 from the fall of 1998? Both witnesses have denied giving these interviews and say that they are fabricated, and it is true that there are certain obvious mistakes in the interviews. However, as the Defence for Haradin Bala points out in paragraph 686 and 711, it seems that at least some of the information in these interviews must have been provided by witnesses L-04 and L-06. Why then are L-04 and L-06 unable to admit that? Given what happened to L-04 and L-06 and the accusations of collaboration made against them, it is hardly surprising that these witnesses would deny any interaction with Serbian officials even years later. Remember the words of Witness L-95, who testified at page 4262 of the transcript of the difficulty of coming to testify in this case. It is striking that in both interviews of L-04 and L-06 by the Serbians in the fall of 1998, they say that they were released from the prison by the order of Celiku, further rebutting the suggestion by the Defence that the victims simply added Limaj to their stories years later. Finally, Your Honours, the identification of Limaj by Ivan Bakrac is striking. Strangely enough, the Defence claims that Ivan Bakrac did not identify Fatmir Limaj as the commander in the prison, and the Defence even goes so far as to claim that this casts doubt on the testimony of Witness L-07. But the opposite is true: Ivan Bakrac did identify Fatmir Limaj. He testified that after he was released from Lapusnik he saw the commander on television, the commander from Lapusnik, and he recognised him to be the commander from the prison. Ivan identified the footage of the funeral march at Carralluke from June 1998, which is contained in Exhibit P35 and which has been authenticated by Fatmir Limaj himself. The person that he recognised in the footage as the commander of Lapusnik is indisputably Fatmir Limaj. In fact, it seems that Ivan did not see the footage of Fatmir Limaj in the funeral march shortly after he left Lapusnik, as he remembered it, but while he was still in Lapusnik. In Vojko Bakrac's interview with the Serbian authorities just after he was released from Lapusnik, which is in evidence as Exhibit P202, and the relevant section is being shown on the Sanction, Vojko Bakrac stated that while in Lapusnik he and Ivan saw footage on the news of "a convoy of KLA members" and that at the "head of the convoy they recognised the commander who had frequently come there and several others from this group." He said he saw this in July 1998. Let's look at the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is undoubtedly the footage that he's talking about and it corroborates Ivan Bakrac's testimony that this is the footage they saw and they recognised on this footage the commander from Lapusnik. When all of the evidence is put together, there can be no question that Fatmir Limaj was the commander that Ivan and Vojko Bakrac saw in Lapusnik, that they recognise in this video in Lapusnik, and who released them from Lapusnik. The Defence seizes on the fact that Ivan Bakrac was unable to pick Fatmir Limaj out of a photo spread when he was interviewed and again in court. But here they are forgetting the testimony of their own expert on identification, Professor Wagenaar. Professor Wagenaar testified at pages 7193 to 94 of the transcript that if a witness sees a suspect with a beard and is later shown a photo spread containing the suspect without a beard, this change can, in some cases, be an impediment to recognition. He even said that the danger in such a case is that you will miss an identification of a guilty person. This is precisely what happened in this case. Ivan Bakrac was able, with absolute certainty, to recognise the image of Fatmir Limaj with the beard from the video. But when he was shown a photograph of Limaj without the beard he could not pick him out. This was true even though he was given a second opportunity to pick Limaj out from the same photo spread in court with Limaj sitting here as one of the three accused in the case, which refutes the suggestion, we submit, that if given the opportunity witnesses will simply and automatically identify those who are in trial in a case. In summary then, the Prosecution submits that the evidence has shown beyond all reasonable doubt, beyond all possible doubt, that Fatmir Limaj was the overall commander of Lapusnik and of the prison there. What about the Isak Musliu? Isak Musliu claimed when he was interviewed during the investigation of this case in 2001, which is in evidence as Exhibit P32, that he was simply a team leader in Lapusnik in charge of, at most, 15 to 16 men. By the time of the pre-trial brief in 2004, however, this number had already increased to between 50 and 60 men. Still now in the final brief he continues to hold on to the claim that he was simply a team leader in Lapusnik; that's simply not true. The evidence had proven beyond all possible doubt that Isak Musliu was the commander of the Celiku 3 unit in Lapusnik. Ruzhdi Karpuzi said so, Witness L-64 said so, Shukri Buja said so in his OTP interview; even Fatmir Limaj confirmed this in his testimony. So what was Isak Musliu's scope of responsibility as commander of the Celiku 3 unit? Musliu contends that there were several units operating in Lapusnik. This is of course highly misleading. The evidence from every witness has shown that the Celiku 3 unit operated in the area below the Peja-Pristina road, and the other units such as the Guri unit, the Lumi unit, and the Pellumbi unit operated in the area above the Peja-Pristina highway. At some point there was also a Pellumbi unit that operated in Kishna Reka to the south of Lapusnik. The area of responsibility of the Celiku 3 unit was confirmed by Ruzhdi Karpuzi, Shukri Buja in his OTP interview, Witness L-64, Dr. Gashi, and others. It is corroborated by documents that were found at Lapusnik contained in Exhibits P244 and P245. Even Elmi Sopi confirmed that when he joined the Pellumbi unit at the end of June 1998, he served across the road, above the Peja-Pristina highway. Celiku 3 was in control of the five fighting positions in Lapusnik: The headquarters; the medical clinic; the kitchen at Gzim Gashi's house; and right across the road from that kitchen, the prison. Isak Musliu also contends that he was just one of the commanders of the Celiku 3 unit. The evidence shows that at most there was just one other commander, Ymer Alushani. As set forth in paragraph 122 of the Prosecution's final brief, the Prosecution submits that Alushani was Musliu's deputy in Lapusnik. But even if it were found that Musliu and Alushani shared command of Celiku 3, it would not change the scope of Musliu's responsibility. So what was the nature of Musliu's command? The evidence shows that he met with important figures when they came to Lapusnik. He commanded the soldiers in fighting, he admitted new soldiers into Celiku 3, he gave permission to soldiers to travel, he gave orders regarding who was in charge of the fighting positions, he had responsibility over discipline, and he ensured the proper operation of the clinic. It is of course impossible to believe that Musliu exercised command over all of these areas and yet had nothing to do with the prison. And in fact, the evidence shows that Isak Musliu had command authority in the prison. As set forth in paragraphs 124 and 125 of the Prosecution's brief, he had power to order prisoners detained or released, and he certainly had authority to give orders to guards within the prison. Musliu claims that Witness L-64 testified that Musliu was not responsible for the prison, but this is in fact not what L-64 said. L-64 said only that he did not know what Musliu's responsibility's were over the prison, but he also made it clear that Musliu was, without question, the commander over Lapusnik and that Musliu was in the prison. In addition, there is overwhelming evidence that Isak Musliu personally participated in brutal beatings and murders within the prison. The Defence challenges the identification of Musliu by Witness L-96. It will, of course, be up to the Trial Chamber to decide if the very specific and clear evidence that Witness L-96 provided about Isak Musliu at Lapusnik was credible. In the submission of the Prosecution, it is impossible to imagine why the witness would have made this story up. Moreover, it is perfectly understandable that this witness did not talk about Musliu in his unfinished and unsigned interview with the Serbian authorities just after he escaped execution or in his first interview with the CCIU. These interviews were preliminary, short, and incomplete, and the witness's focus, quite understandably, was on what had happened in Berisa. Needless to say, the alibi of Isak Musliu, claiming that he was not even in Lapusnik when L-96 was there, simply never materialised. Moreover, the evidence of Witness L-96 is hardly the only evidence that Musliu beat prisoners in Lapusnik. Other prisoners testified that Qerqiz beat prisoners regularly, and one victim learned from a prison from Musliu's own village that Qerqiz was Isak Musliu, and several prisoners gave descriptions matching Musliu. Taken together, the Prosecution submits that the evidence establishes beyond all reasonable doubt that Isak Musliu was the commander of Celiku 3 and of the prison in Lapusnik and that he personally participated in crimes there. Your Honour, I'm not sure when you would like to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In another 10 to 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Finally, Haradin Bala. The evidence shows that Haradin Bala was Shala, the guard in the prison in Lapusnik who also participated in beatings and murder. There can be no doubt that the guard in the prison was in fact Shala and that this Shala participated in the crimes charged against him. The only issue is: Was Shala Haradin Bala? In the submission of the Prosecution, there can be no doubt about this. First, Haradin Bala was identified in photo spreads by two completely independent witnesses, L-96 and Ivan Bakrac. These two witnesses were at Lapusnik at different times and were interviewed by different investigators. There is no evidence that they have ever spoken with each other. Each of these two witnesses picked out Haradin Bala immediately from the photo spread and said that it was Shala. It is impossible that this could have been a mistake or a mere coincidence. The Defence makes a number of specious attacks on these identifications hoping, no doubt, that if enough mud is thrown something will stick. The Defence contends over and over again in paragraphs 626, 637, and 650 that after his release from Lapusnik, Ivan Bakrac searched the Internet for somebody responsible; that's simply not the evidence. The evidence is that Ivan Bakrac was simply looking for information about Kosovo on the Internet, and this very fact was acknowledged again and again in the Defence counsel's own questions to Ivan Bakrac at transcript pages 1481, 1491, 1501, and 1528. The Defence also suggests that Ivan Bakrac gave two or three statements before he identified Bala; well, that's not true either. In fact, the evidence shows that while Ivan was present when his father was interviewed just after their release from Lapusnik and added, at most, one or two pieces of information, he himself was interviewed for the very first time by the OTP, and at that time he identified Haradin Bala from the photo spread. With respect to L-96, the Defence suggests in paragraph 781 that the witness required more time in order to make the identification of Shala; nothing could be further from the truth. It is hard to imagine how anybody could forget the testimony in this courtroom of Witness L-96 about how he picked out Haradin Bala immediately and without hesitation. The Defence also criticises in paragraph 875 the instruction given to L-96 by the investigator. First off, the Defence misstates the instruction that the investigator gave to the witnesses. The investigator did not ask the witnesses, as the Defence alleges, which of the faces they saw was Shala in the photo spread; rather, the investigator asked the witnesses, as set forth in paragraph 11 of P259, if they saw Shala in any of the pictures. Moreover, such an instruction telling the witness which suspect the photo board was for is precisely what is recommended by the Defence expert on identification, Professor Wagenaar. Finally, the Defence argues that L-96's identification was tainted by information that he received from others. But none of the information that the witness received could have in any way assisted him in selecting, immediately and without hesitation, the photograph of Haradin Bala from the photo spread. The Defence suggests that the identifications of L-96 and Ivan Bakrac should be outweighed by witnesses who picked nobody out of the Haradin Bala photo spread, but at the same time the Defence quite properly acknowledges the testimony of Professor Wagenaar, that identifications are not simply a matter of adding up the score. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution submits that the witnesses who failed to pick anybody out of photo spreads were, generally speaking, more traumatised, more broken by the experience of being in Lapusnik, and for this reason were less willing or less able to assist the investigation in this case. The failure of these witnesses to identify somebody simply does not cancel out the certain and powerful identifications of L-96 and Ivan Bakrac. Your Honour, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a significant point in your order, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that event we will break now, resuming I think at 5 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I continue, I must make a correction of a misstatement which was brought to my attention by Mr. Younis, covering my back until the very end. At page 20, line 4, I said -- I referred to "P23 and P24." I should have said P203 and P204.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before the break I was talking about the identifications of Haradin Bala by witnesses L-96 and Ivan Bakrac. The Defence also attacks the photo spread procedures used by the investigators. I will not repeat here all of the arguments made by the Prosecution in its final brief on this subject; however, the Prosecution submits that the photo spreads and the procedures were in fact reliable. The one procedure that should have been followed, which wasn't, is that witnesses should have been told that the suspect may not be in the photo spread. But the evidence is that the only consequence of failing to follow this instruction is that it could have caused the witnesses, if they did not recognise anybody, to guess. There is no evidence, however, that this occurred in this case. Ivan Bakrac identified Haradin Bala from the photo spread, but he did not identify anyone from the other photo spreads; he did not guess. Vojko Bakrac did not identify anybody from the photo spreads; he did not guess. These results positively refute the unfounded allegation by the Defence that Investigator Lehtinen guided the witnesses to choose a paragraph in the photo spreads, which appears in paragraph 889 of the final brief. Witness L-96 identified all three accused in this case, but he did not identify anybody from the photo spread containing a picture of Agim Murtezi, again demonstrating that he did not guess. In isolation, the failure to tell a witness that the suspect may not be in the photo spread does not, in our submission, undermine the identification. In all other respects, the photo spreads and the procedures were fair and there is no evidence whatsoever of suggestiveness, either in the photo spreads or in the procedures. The Defence also alleges, falsely, that the investigators failed to record negative identifications. The record in this case establishes precisely the opposite with respect to all three investigators, and reference is made to transcript page 4949 for Mr. Kereakes, paragraph 15 of Exhibit P258 for Mr. Lehtinen, and paragraph 17 of exhibit P259 for Mr. Manthey. Obviously the Prosecution has disclosed all positive and negative identifications to the Defence, regardless of whether they were led in evidence. And in our submission, it is entirely improper for the Defence to raise the ghost of negative identifications that may not be in the record in this case, as it would be improper for the Prosecution to ask the Court to speculate about other positive identifications that are not in the record. Finally, the Defence contends that in evaluating the identifications the Court should focus on the photo spread procedures but not on the circumstances under which the witnesses saw the accused in this case. The law, however, is the opposite. In the United States, for example, the law is that even when there is a showing of suggestiveness in the pre-trial identification procedure, something which has not been established here, the identification will not be excluded where there is a strong basis for the identification, meaning sufficient viewing time, favourable conditions, degree of attention, and the like. This law is set forth in detail in footnote 544 of the Prosecution's final brief, and I will not repeat it here. In the view of the Prosecution, the two identifications of L-96 and Ivan Bakrac alone prove that Shala was Haradin Bala. There is no other explanation for how these two independent witnesses could have each picked out, with certainty and without hesitation, Haradin Bala. But of course there is much more. There is the testimony of L-64, who says that Haradin Bala was in fact the guard at Lapusnik, at the prison, and the testimony of Dr. Gashi, who knew Haradin Bala from long before the war and testified that he was in fact in Lapusnik in July -- June and July of 1998. The Defence suggests that L-64 was confused about Haradin Bala, but L-64 explained that in his first interviews with the OTP he sought to protect Haradin Bala. Nonetheless, even though L-64 wanted to protect Bala and in court L-64 continued to say that he did not believe that Bala had committed any crimes, he clearly stated in his interviews with the OTP and in court that Bala was in fact a guard in the prison in Lapusnik. It was Bala. The Defence also says that there is no mention of Shala or of the prison in the diary of Witness L-64. It is hardly a surprise that L-64 did not talk about the prison in his diary. It was plainly the dirty little secret of Lapusnik, and L-64 himself testified that he was not interested in writing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Apparently there's French interpretation in the English channel. I will say something to make sure it's okay. Besides, what possible conclusion can be drawn from the fact that the prison and Shala are not in the diary? Is there really any doubt that there was a prison in Lapusnik and that Shala was a guard there? No. The fact that L-64 did not write about this in his diary hardly undermines these facts, and it certainly does not undermine L-64's reluctant testimony that Haradin Bala was Shala, the guard in the prison in Lapusnik. With respect to Dr. Gashi, the Defence contends that Dr. Gashi was wrong about when he opened his clinic at the Ferat Sopi compound and when he saw Haradin Bala there. They point to a previous interview of Dr. Gashi, which did not result in a signed statement, and to the testimony of Ferat Sopi. The evidence, however, shows that in Dr. Gashi's first interview, during which he himself admits he was not cooperative and not completely truthful, he said that he opened the clinic in May or June of 1998. The evidence also shows that in this interview, Dr. Gashi did not focus with precision on the particular dates and events during the month of May. When Dr. Gashi did focus on the exact chronology, he testified without any doubt that the clinic opened at the beginning of June or, at the earliest, on the last day of May. And this is exactly corroborated by the apparently complete record of injections given at the clinic, which is in evidence as Exhibit P127. Dr. Gashi also testified that he saw Bala in the clinic in June -- Correction. That's Exhibit P217, not 127. Dr. Gashi also testified that he saw Bala in the clinic in June or July of 1998. On the other hand, the testimony of Ferat Sopi was nothing but equivocal concerning the date the clinic opened, and his testimony on this subject is certainly less reliable than the testimony of Dr. Gashi. Moreover, the evidence is that before testifying, Ferat Sopi read the transcript of Dr. Gashi's testimony in this court, which was published in the newspaper and which is in evidence at P252, and which, it is important to say, is different from what was read out to Ferat Sopi by the Defence in re-direct examination. And therefore, I would urge the Court to look closely at that exhibit and the translation of that exhibit. And the evidence is that Ferat Sopi stated to the investigator that the testimony that he read of Dr. Gashi in that newspaper article, which is in evidence, was accurate. Finally, and this is very important, the clinic was not the only place where Dr. Gashi saw Haradin Bala. He also testified that he saw him once or twice while going to the kitchen at Gzim Gashi's compound in June or July of 1998. The Defence itself concedes in paragraph 834 that Haradin Bala worked in the kitchen in Gzim Gashi's compound. However, the evidence from Elmi Sopi and Witness L-64 establishes without any doubt that Gzim Gashi's compound was not used as a kitchen until after the 29th of May, 1998. The evidence establishes, therefore, that Haradin Bala did not leave Lapusnik as he contends, but in fact he stayed in June and July and was a guard in the prison. And there is more evidence proving that Haradin Bala was Shala. The other victims at Lapusnik who testified provided descriptions of Shala that match Haradin Bala. Remember, the evidence is that there were just two Shalas at Lapusnik: Haradin Bala and Ruzhdi Karpuzi. This is your pool of suspects. The descriptions match Haradin Bala; they do not match at all Ruzhdi Karpuzi. Further, Witness L-07 testified that he met Shala at a petrol station after the war and learned from him that his name was Haradin Bala. There is no reason why this witness would have made up this testimony. Bala was also identified in court by witnesses L-06, L-07, L-10, and L-12. It is true that ordinarily so-called dock IDs should carry little weight. Here, however, as the Prosecution argues in paragraph 157 of its brief, in light of the prolonged and varied exposure of the victims to Shala at Lapusnik, the court identifications of Haradin Bala should carry corroborative weight. Finally, Your Honours, there is Haradin Bala's alibi to consider. The Prosecution agrees with the statement of the Defence in paragraph 30 of their brief that: "Even if the Trial Chamber declines to accept the truthfulness of the narratives of Haradin Bala's alibi Defence witnesses," the burden is still on the Prosecution to prove Bala's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. That is true. However, it is also the case, it is submitted, that a false alibi, not an alibi that fails to materialise, but a false alibi can be considered as evidence of guilt. In support of this proposition, the Prosecution offers the cases of United States versus Fortes, which is reported at 619, F.2d 108, in particular page 123, note 6; that is a case from the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals in the United States from 1980. And the case of People versus Ficarrota, 92, New York 2d 244, in particular page 250, a 1997 case of the Court of Appeals of New York, which is the highest court in the state of New York. Haradin Bala's alibi is indeed false. Look at its various versions. In Bala's pre-trial brief in paragraph 4, which was filed a year and a half after he was arrested after he had had considerable time to consider the details of his whereabouts during the summer of 1998, he stated that on the 8th of May 1998 he was in his home village of Korretice when he heard fighting in Lapusnik, and that he went from his home village, Korretice, to Lapusnik to fight. In Bala's statement to the Court, he said the same thing at page 6912. In the final brief, however, relying on the testimony of Kadri Dugoli, the Defence asserts in paragraphs 831 and 832 that Bala had moved his familiar to Nekovce before the fighting in Lapusnik and that he was in Nekovce when he heard the fighting in Lapusnik and went to Lapusnik from Nekovce. In the pre-trial brief, Bala also says that he stayed in Lapusnik at most 15 days, which would have meant the 23rd of May, and that he participated in the fighting of the 17th to 18th of May. This claim was repeated in the alibi notice and in court by Bala himself with respect to the 15 days, or two weeks, at transcript page 6913. Elmi Sopi testified, however, that Bala was still in Lapusnik on the 29th of May and that he participated in the very important battle on that day, a fact that is simply not accounted for anywhere in Bala's alibi. Next, Bala claims in the pre-trial brief that after he left Lapusnik he went to Klecke where he worked at a training camp for a short time and then went to work in a warehouse in Luznica. In the alibi notice, this account is more vague, stating only that after Bala left Lapusnik he worked in Luznica and Klecke, without specifying when. In Bala's statement to the Court, he said that he went from Lapusnik to Luznica, not to Klecke as had been stated in the pre-trial brief. In fact, there is no mention of Klecke at all. The final brief ends up taking both approaches. In paragraph 614 it states that Bala was in Klecke, Luznica, and Javor after he left Lapusnik. In paragraphs 835 and 838, however, it is just Luznica. Of course, there is no witness who saw him either in Luznica or in Klecke during this time period, not a single one. And who should have seen him in Klecke? Well, Fatmir Limaj, of course, who was the commander in Klecke and who states in paragraph 580 of the final brief: "Regularly turned away civilians and refused to expand KLA ranks" in Klecke, taking a "careful and prudent approach" to expanding his unit in Klecke. However, Fatmir Limaj said in court that the first time he -- he claimed in court that the first time he ever met Haradin Bala was when the arrests occurred in this case. Even he did not say that he saw Haradin Bala in Klecke during the summer of 1998, though the characterisation of his careful control over his unit in Klecke, which is in paragraph 580, would suggest that he must have known if Haradin Bala was there. The simple fact is: Haradin Bala was not in Klecke, he was not in Luznica, he was in Lapusnik. Bala also claims now, for the first time in the final brief, that his medical condition rendered him incapable of committing the crimes alleged in this indictment. This claim appears in paragraphs 617, 810, and 845 of the Defence brief. Of course, this new claim is in contradiction to what Bala's Defence counsel said in the opening of their case, where it was said at page 6899 of the transcript that: "We cannot say that it would have been physically impossible for Haradin Bala to perform the actions that he is accused of performing." Of course that's true. There has been no evidence in this case showing that it would have been physically impossible for Haradin Bala to have committed the crimes. A bad idea, perhaps, but a bad idea for lots of reasons. Bala's alibi is filled with other contradictions that are set forth in more detail in the Prosecution's final brief. The alibi is false, and of course Haradin Bala knows it's false. He wasn't in Luznica, he wasn't in Klecke, he was in Lapusnik, a guard in the prison Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in June and July of 1998. This has been proven, we submit beyond any doubt -- any reasonable doubt, and the false alibi is evidence of Haradin Bala's consciousness of guilt. Now, Your Honours, I will turn to Mr. Black, who will address the evidence about the particular crimes charged in this case, after which Mr. Nicholls will address the issues of armed conflict and widespread and systematic attack. Then I will conclude, likely tomorrow, next session, tomorrow on the issue of sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. May it please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- the Trial Chamber. As stated by Mr. Whiting, the Prosecution submits that it has proven its case regarding all counts, as alleged in the second amended indictment. There is one small exception, which we've noted in our final brief: The Prosecution concedes that the evidence did not sustain the count of murder with regard to Sinisa Blagojevic. However, with that one exception, the Prosecution contends that all of the crimes in the indictment, the imprisonment, the conditions of detention, the beatings and the torture, and every murder identified in the indictment and in annexes I, II, and III, has been proven beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence establishing those crimes is addressed at length in our final brief, and I don't intend to repeat that detailed effort here, nevertheless we do think it appropriate to publicly summarise how the evidence has supported the allegations in the indictment and to address some of the issues raised by the accused in their joint final brief. First and fundamentally, the evidence has established beyond any possible doubt that there was in fact a prison camp operated by the KLA, located in the village of Lapusnik. The Trial Chamber heard direct evidence from a number of survivors of the camp, including witnesses L-04, L-06, L-07, L-10, L-12, L-96, and the Bakracs. Their testimony plainly established that they were held in a prison camp, that their captors were members of the KLA, and that the camp was located in Lapusnik, specifically in the compound which is labelled Compound A in Prosecution Exhibit's P5 and P6. Significantly, that victim testimony regarding the camp was strongly corroborated by other trial evidence. For example, Shukri Buja testified that he went to Lapusnik and arranged for the release of a detainee. Witness L-64, another KLA insider, testified that he personally visited the camp in June and July of 1998. Further corroboration was provided by documentary evidence found in Lapusnik after it fell to the Serbian forces at the end of July 1998. Those documents are included, for the most part, in sealed Prosecution Exhibit P244 and in its public version, Exhibit P245. That evidence was admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis, with the agreement of the Defence. However, in their final brief, the Defence argue that the source and authenticity of the documents is unclear; that is not correct. The source and authenticity of the documents is addressed in the statement of Witness 103 at the beginning of Exhibit P244/P245. The provenance of the documents is also addressed in a memo found at tab 1 to that exhibit, which is dated 18 August 1998, approximately three weeks after the seizure of the documents in Lapusnik. Some of the documents have also been independently authenticated by other witnesses in court. For instance, tab 2 [sic] is also Exhibit P129, which was authenticated by Ruzhdi Karpuzi and by Witness L-64. Dr. Zeqir Gashi authenticated a number of documents found at Lapusnik, including prescriptions, medical histories, and a list of injections from his clinic there. Those documents, marked Prosecution Exhibits 215, 216, and 217, are also addressed in P245. The Prosecution thus submits that the evidence of the existence of a KLA camp in Lapusnik is overwhelming. As noted earlier by Mr. Whiting, the Defence even stopped cross-examining Prosecution witnesses on this issue towards the end of the Prosecution case, and there's a reference in our final brief at footnote 349. However, in the final brief of the Defence the argument is resurrected at paragraph 178, where they suggest not only that there was no KLA camp in Lapusnik, but that the KLA was incapable of running any prison camp, period. Fatmir Limaj has also adamantly denied the existence of the camp from early in his proceedings as well as in his oral testimony before the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, we submit that the Defence position that there was no KLA camp in Lapusnik simply cannot be reconciled with the evidence. The Trial Chamber also heard direct evidence from the victims about their unlawful imprisonment in the camp and inhumane conditions which they suffered there. One victim who testified before the Trial Chamber was Witness L-06, who described the conditions in the storage room, which was marked A5 in Prosecution Exhibits P5 and P6. The relevant testimony is at pages 994 to 999 of the transcript, and it's fairly long so I won't read it out in its entirety, but I'd like to highlight a couple of points addressed. In essence on page 994, Mr. Whiting asks Witness L-06 to describe the room in which he was held. On the next page he says: "It was 2 metres by 3 metres." It had a floor made of concrete with manure on the floor. He says there was water leaking from the ceiling, that it had one very small window. And then the following questions ensue: "Q. What was the temperature in that room? "A. The temperature, I don't know how to tell you, well, if someone had set fire to the place. It was very hot. "Q. Did you have enough air in that room? "A. No. No, what air? "Q. Witness, what did you do when you needed to use the toilet? "A. We never went to a bathroom. There was a toilet inside there for two or three weeks. Then they brought a kind of bucket, and that's where we had to relieve ourselves. "Q. During the first two or three weeks, where did you relieve yourselves? "A. At the door in the corner."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING ASKS
utterances.text: "Q. On the floor? "A. Yes, on the floor there, behind the door. "Q. When there was a bucket, was the bucket emptied regularly? "A. No. When it became full, sometimes it overflowed. When they felt like emptying it, they came and emptied it. When they didn't, it stayed like that, full." Mr. Whiting continues to ask the witness about food. He says: "Q. How often were you given food when you were in that room? "A. Food? Mostly we went without food than with food. Three or four days we stayed without food. Sometimes they gave us food, sometimes for 24 hours they didn't. Sometimes they brought us food... but for three or four days we stayed -- we went without food." Then he explains that when they were given food it amounted to pasta or a piece of bread. He said there was enough water. And when Mr. Whiting asked him about who brought the water the answer was: "A. Shala brought the water." Another question on page 997, and this is the last passage from this transcript: "Q. Did a doctor ever come to care for any of the people in that room? "A. No, there was no doctor. "Q. Were you ever allowed to leave the room and walk around the yard? "A. No, only Shala sometimes opened the door to air the room in the evening after sunset. So we could get out a little bit and we went in again. "Q. Did that happen every day? "A. No, once a week, once every three or four days." Your Honour, Witness L-06's description was corroborated by other evidence. In fact, every victim who came to testify testified about the horrible conditions at the camp, and in fact the brutality of those conditions was also testified to by Witness L-06, himself a KLA insider, a member of the Celiku 3 unit -- L-64. Sorry. L-64 was the KLA insider. As set forth in the Prosecution's final brief, we submit that severe beatings and torture were fundamental characteristics of the Lapusnik prison camp. The Trial Chamber heard testimony from a number of witnesses who were themselves beaten at the camp, including witnesses L-04, L-12, and L-96. Indeed, the victim evidence revealed a clear pattern in which beatings occurred on a regular basis, essentially every night. Prisoners were sometimes beaten in the rooms in which they were held, other times they were taken out for beatings. In one witness's words: "Nobody knew whose turn it was to be beaten." The Trial Chamber also heard powerful evidence about specific incidents of beatings, for example the torture of Stamen Genov, a young medic in the Yugoslav army who was taken off of a bus along with the Bakracs and eventually murdered in the camp. Vojko and Ivan Bakrac described in detail how Genov was mercilessly beaten upon his arrival at the camp. Vojko Bakrac further described how at the end of that beating a soldier closely matching the description of Isak Musliu threatened to cut off Genov's genitals with a knife while Genov begged for mercy. Another striking example of the combination of physical and psychological torture at the camp was an incident described by Vojko Bakrac when he and Ivan were taken downstairs in building A1 for "tea." And I'd like to show you a clip of his testimony. Mr. Younis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING ASKS
utterances.text: "MR. BLACK: "Q. -- the first one that you were taken to at a farm. "A. Yes, on one occasion we were called to go down there. We had tea. We sat there. "Q. Did anything else happen besides having tea? "A. Yes. There was an unpleasant situation for me and for my son. We had to watch as other men were beaten. "Q. I know it's unpleasant, but I'm going to ask you to describe that occasion for the Trial Chamber. First, do you remember how many men were there being beaten? "A. They brought four or five of them. I don't know the exact number, but it wasn't more than five. They lined them up and started beating them. They would beat every one of them for five or ten minutes, slapping them, kicking them, hitting them on their legs. One of them was unable to stand at all. At any rate, they were beaten up. "Q. Did you recognise any of the soldiers who participated in the beating? "A. Yes. The same man that beat Genov beat these people. I'm referring to the first day when we arrived there, in that facility. "Q. Was this person armed now on this -- this occasion that you're describing right now? "A. He had a pistol. "Q. Did he do anything with that pistol? "A. Yes, I remember that. When they stopped beating them, he handed a pistol to one of these men and he told him to kill the others. The man lifted the pistol up and put him next to a person's forehead. They were crying, begging for mercy. Then this first man took the pistol, put it next to the man -- another man's forehead and fired it, but it was empty. I think it was some kind of a psychological torture."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think we're done with the Sanction for the moment. Thank you. Your Honours, it must be noted that many of the victims of physical violence in the Lapusnik camp were extremely vulnerable. For example, Mus Musliu and Witness 12 were both elderly men. Nevertheless, the evidence is that Mus Musliu was beaten by Shala in building A1 and Witness L12 was beaten by Shala, this time in a barn in the presence of Qerqiz. Another example is that of Shaban Hoti, a retired professor from Pristina who was detained while working as an interpreter for Russian journalists who were covering the conflict. The Trial Chamber heard from Oleg Safiulin, one of the Russian journalists, how Hoti was savagely beaten after their detention along the Pristina-Peja road, which incidentally corroborates the testimony of another witness who saw Hoti arrive at the Lapusnik camp in a very bad condition. Once there, and the next day as well, soldiers kicked and jumped on Hoti until, in one witness's words: "You had no idea whether he was alive or dead." It is significant that the testimonial evidence of serious beatings in this case was corroborated by expert scientific evidence, specifically by the expert reports of Jose Pablo Baraybar, which is Prosecution Exhibit 111, and the report of George Maat, Exhibit P200, as well as by Dr. Maat's viva voce testimony before Your Honours. Forensic examinations by those two experts revealed that the remains of several victims from the camp showed signs of ante-mortem injuries, that is injuries that occurred before death, which were completely consistent with severe beatings, as described by surviving victims. For example, several witnesses testified that a detainee named Shyqyri Zymeri suffered a broken leg while at the camp and that he had to be carried by other prisoners during the march to Berisa, where he was murdered on 26 July 1998. Zymeri's body was recovered from the execution site in 2001 and it was identified by DNA analysis performed by the International Commission on Missing Persons. Forensic examination of those remains by Baraybar and Maat showed that Zymeri had suffered a fracture of the right tibia - in other words, a broken leg - approximately three weeks before his death. And it's important to lay this out clearly. Shyqyri Zymeri was kidnapped on the 26th of June 1998. He was murdered one month later on the 26th of July 1998. That means that three weeks before his death at the time his leg was broken, according to Dr. Maat, he was being held in the Lapusnik prison camp. The science precisely corroborates the witness testimony. Now, I would note that Dr. Maat's evidence, together with other victim testimony, also established that Emin Emini suffered fractures to his sternum and to several ribs while detained in the camp and Lutfi Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Xhemshiti suffered two broken ribs approximately two weeks before his death, again while he was detained in Lapusnik. Incidentally, Your Honours, there was no evidence that Shyqyri Zymeri, Emin Emini or Lutfi Xhemshiti received any medical treatment for their broken bones, which obviously, particularly in the case of Zymeri, must have the excruciatingly painful. To the contrary, the evidence is that seriously injured prisoners such as Srboljub Miladinovic, who was shot in the legs, received no medical care, even though, Your Honours, we know from several witnesses that there was an operational medical clinic operating a matter of two or three hundred metres away in the compound of Ferat Sopi. Medical care was available, but it was not offered. Your Honour, under the circumstances, the wilful denial of medical care - and it's clearly wilful - the wilful denial of medical services to seriously injured prisoners constitutes torture. It is hardly surprising, given the intensity of the physical violence of the camp, that many men died there. The Trial Chamber received evidence from several sources about murders in the camp from surviving prisoners, from a KLA insider, and from expert witnesses. The Defence position, both before and during trial, was that they "could not gainsay" the deaths of the murder victims identified in the indictment. In their final brief, however, that position has changed, and the Defence argue in paragraph 155 that where no body has been recovered "the Prosecution has failed to prove anything beyond the disappearance of these individuals." In fact, with the exception of Sinisa Blagojevic, whom I mentioned earlier, the Prosecution has put forward evidence sufficient for the Trial Chamber to find that every victim named in Counts 7 and 8 and Annexes I and II of the indictment was killed in or in close connection with the Lapusnik camp. First, in several instances the Trial Chamber has heard directly from eyewitnesss to the murders or to events closely related to the murders. For example, Ajet Gashi. The Trial Chamber heard direct evidence about his execution, which was corroborated by 92 bis evidence from a family member of his, by newspaper accounts of the murder and of the discovery of his body, and also by forensic examination of the body itself. Another example is Agim Ademi. Ademi was last seen alive by his fellow prisoners when he was taken by Qerqiz from the cowshed. And the cowshed, by the way, is marked A6 on Prosecution Exhibits 5 and 6. The evidence shows that detainees were later forced by Shala to bury the dead bodies of three men, one of whom was recognised as Agim Ademi. The Defence erroneously claim at paragraph 170 of their final brief that Ademi was never even placed at the camp by the evidence. However, they do later refer to the account of Ademi's burial as one of the reasons why a particular document obtained from the Serbian authorities must be genuine. And you will find that at paragraph 686 of the brief. In any event, we submit that the evidence is overwhelming that Agim Ademi was murdered by the KLA with the participation on some level of both Isak Musliu and Haradin Bala. Third, we have the murder of Fehmi Xhema, also known as Fehmi Tafa. Xhema's death was witnessed firsthand by two fellow prisoners. Their accounts were largely similar, although they do differ in one important aspect. Witness L-10 testified that Xhema was taken out of the storage room by Shala and Qerqiz just before his death, while Witness L-06 testified that it was Ramadan Behluli and Ali Gashi who took Xhema out of the storage room. Now, we have set out in our final brief, and you can look at footnote 732, why we submit that the Trial Chamber could find beyond reasonable doubt that Witness L-10's version is accurate. However, we submit that this is ultimately a factual matter for the Trial Chamber. But what is notable is that both witnesses implicate Shala in the immediate aftermath of Xhema's final beating, denying, or according to L-06 eventually reluctantly providing, water to the dying man, and participating in the removal of his body some days after his death. The Defence have argued several points in their brief that the autopsy report of Fehmi Xhema, which is found at Prosecution Exhibit P227, somehow invalidates the testimonial evidence of his murder. At paragraph 734 they go so far as to say that parts of the witnesses' accounts are "undeniably false." However, we invite you to look at the autopsy report because all it shows is that Xhema possibly received a gunshot wound to the thorax, or chest, around the time of his death. There is no support whatsoever, by the way, for the Defence claim that "a man with a gunshot wound to the thorax cannot speak or would have extreme difficulty speaking." That is not supported by any evidence on the record and I would say that it's not supported by common sense, either. If Xhema was indeed shot before he died in the storage room, we submit that it is entirely plausible that Witnesses L-06 and L-10 simply did not notice that, in addition to the severe beatings which he had suffered, Xhema had also sustained a gunshot wound. It is understandable that they would have been concerned more with the ultimate issue of whether he would live or die than with the specifics of how he was mortally injured. Do the Defence really suggest that Witness L-06 and Witness L-10 made up their story? Could anyone believe that they were mistaken about Fehmi Xhema literally dying in their arms? We submit that despite the differences in their accounts, the core of their evidence is both consistent and credible. Moreover, whether Xhema was beaten to death or shot to death, what is clear from the evidence is that he was murdered in the Lapusnik prison camp and that Haradin Bala, at least, was personally involved.
