In the same or perhaps the next category are the murders of Jefta Petkovic and Zvonko Marinkovic. Like Agim Ademi, these men were both seen alive for the last time being taken by Qerqiz from the cowshed. The two dead bodies that were later buried along with Agim Ademi were described as approximately 50 to 55 years of age and 35 years of age, which matches the ages of Marinkovic and Petkovic. Moreover, one of the bodies, according to the witnesses, had a serious injury to the head, which is again consistent with other evidence, in this case the forensic examination of the bodies of Marinkovic and Petkovic which were discovered in a secondary grave site in 2004. You can find that evidence in Exhibit P111, which is the expert report of Jose Pablo Baraybar. Here again, we submit that the Defence is simply incorrect when they state at paragraph 169 of their final brief that no witnesses placed these two men at the camp; the evidence in fact shows much more than that. And the Trial Chamber should find that they were murdered after being taken out by Isak Musliu and that they were buried in a remote location at the direction of Haradin Bala. The bodies of the remaining murder victims identified in Annex I and Annex II have not been recovered; that much is true. However, the Defence is incorrect to suggest that their deaths must therefore be dismissed from this case. As we set forth in our final brief, it has been held, notably in the Krnojelac case, that it is not necessary to produce a body in order to demonstrate that victims have been killed. Krnojelac set out a number of factors to be considered as you weigh the circumstantial evidence and we have addressed all those factors in our final brief. In essence, we submit that the Trial Chamber can find beyond a reasonable doubt that all these men were killed at the camp or in close connection with the camp, based on the following evidence: Number one, the fact that each man was last seen alive in the camp; number two, the fact that none has been seen or heard from by his family in the seven years since he disappeared; and three - and this is very important - the pattern of crimes at the camp, because these disappearances did not occur in a vacuum. The evidence shows torture and murder of Serb and Albanian civilians and the burial and abandonment of victims' bodies in unmarked and sometimes concealed locations. Your Honours, often the last people to accept the death of a missing person are the family members of that person. Ljiljana Mitrovic, the widow of Slobodan Mitrovic, also called Boban, came before Your Honours and testified eloquently about her own reluctant conclusion that her husband had been killed. The next clip shows the last part of her testimony. Mr. Younis, could you show that on the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: "MR. CAYLEY: "Q. I want to ask you one final question. Six years have now passed since Boban disappeared. Today as you sit in the courtroom, do you believe him to be alive or dead? "A. I would like to be proven wrong and to be given a chance to apologise to everyone. But I do believe that he was killed, and that is why I'm here because I want justice to prevail. And that those who committed that, that they be brought before justice and be held responsible."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We're finished with Sanction. Thank you. In summary, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber has heard substantial evidence regarding the murders alleged in Counts 7 and 8 of the indictment, and we ask the Trial Chamber to find that all of the named victims with the exception of Blagojevic were murdered in the camp or directly in connection with the camp. I'll turn now to the events at Berisa, where ten men were executed on July 1998. The Trial Chamber heard directly from a survivor of the Berisa execution, Witness L-96, who described the entire episode in detail. This witness's evidence which was convincing on its face was also corroborated in a number of ways by other evidence. First, of course, several witnesses testified about being taken out of their rooms in the camp and marched up to Berisa by Haradin Bala and another guard named Murrizi, exactly as described by Witness L-96. Second, and arguably more important, Witness L-96's account was powerfully corroborated by the scientific evidence of a number of other witnesses. In 2001 L-96 led investigators to the site where he said the execution took place. Thereafter, the bodies of all but one of the victims he named were subsequently exhumed from that site. The identities of Emin Emini, Ibush Hamza, Hyzri Hajrizi, Shaban Hoti, Hasan Hoxha, Safet Hysenaj, Bashkim Rashiti, Lutfi Xhemshiti, and Shyqyri Zymeri were confirmed by DNA analysis performed by the International Commission on Missing Persons. In other words, Your Honours, the people who Witness L-96 said would be there were there. Forensic examination of the bodies recovered from Berisa by Baraybar and Maat also revealed ante-mortem and perimortem injuries - again, that means injuries inflicted before and around the time of death - which corroborated the testimony of L-96 and other Prosecution witnesses. There was evidence of severe beatings, and I gave the examples of in the cases of Shyqyri Zymeri, Emin Emini, and Lutfi Xhemshiti earlier. There is also evidence of gunshot wounds at the time of death. Moreover, Your Honours, as set out in our final brief, expert ballistics evidence found at Exhibit P113 confirmed that spent ammunition recovered at the Berisa site was fired from two Kalashnikov automatic weapons, which matches exactly with the testimony of Witness L-96 and others who said that Haradin Bala and the third soldier there were each carrying the Kalashnikovs. In sum, Witness L-96's evidence regarding the events of 26 July 1998 was corroborated on all of the following points: Release from the camp, the march to Berisa, the site of the killings, the identities of those men released, the identities of those men killed, the make of the murder weapon, Shala's participation, and Fatmir Limaj's participation, which I will turn to in a moment. First, however, the Defence final brief emphasises that Hetem Rexhaj's body has never been recovered, and we suggests that this is a serious problem with Witness L-96's evidence. It is striking that with an account as overwhelming corroborated as that of Witness L-96 the Defence nonetheless latch on to this one issue as supposed proof that the entire account is incredible. We submit that there are at least two reasonable explanations for the fact that Hetem Rexhaj's body has never been found. First, the body may well have been moved. There is other evidence in this case of the use of secondary graves. And as the Trial Chamber is aware there is compelling reason why Rexhaj's body might have been removed and the others left. Second, the body may be nearby and it simply has not been found. The location of this execution site is very rugged and isolated. The Trial Chamber will remember that Witness L-96 in which he described the thick underbrush through which he had to go as he escaped the execution. There is also evidence that the shallow grave at Berisa allowed scavenging animals to disrupt the grave site. I do note that the body of Hasan Hoxha was found many months after the other bodies, although it was found in the same basic exhumation site, due to precisely these types of problems. Your Honours, in any event, it does not ultimately matter why Hetem Rexhaj's body has not been found. Witness L-96 saw him murdered by Haradin Bala and two other KLA soldiers, and that eyewitness evidence is plainly sufficient for a finding that he was murdered as alleged. I turn now to Fatmir Limaj's involvement in the Berisa murders. The Defence suggest that the only evidence of Limaj's involvement consist of L-96 testimony, which they attack, and the release papers which they also question. Dealing first with L-96, as I have stated, his account is strongly corroborated on a number of other details and we submit that his evidence alone is sufficient to prove Limaj's involvement. This is particularly so when one considers the conditions under which he saw Limaj on the 26th of July, 1998. It was daytime. He was a short distance away from where Limaj and Bala were speaking, he testified about 7 to 8 metres, and he saw Limaj for an extended time, perhaps as many as 5 minutes according to his testimony. These are excellent viewing conditions, ideal for a subsequent identification. Witness L-96's account, however, is further supported by the evidence that the first group of prisoners were released on the order of Celiku. Several witnesses testified about this, either saying that they were told this information or that they were given release papers on which it was actually written. Now, while the details of this testimony do vary slightly, seen as a whole, we submit that this evidence is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. powerful corroboration for the fact that Shala consulted with Fatmir Limaj on the march and took orders regarding the fate of the prisoners. Now, while the Defence complained that the release papers were never tendered into evidence, in fact the record shows that the papers were given to Luan and Shukri Buja in Kroimire. You can find that reference at page 1199 of the transcript. I also note that the Serb statements of Witnesses L-04 and L-06, on which the Defence place so many weight in another context, confirm these release papers. Finally on another issue, the Prosecution submits that the evidence of Limaj's involvement in the Berisa events must be considered in light of the other evidence of his command position. For example, Witness L-95 testified that in that same time frame unit commanders were reporting to Limaj, which shows that he was actively monitoring the situation and he was in command of the area. Secondly, we submit that it's highly improbable that Shala would have acted on his own in deciding the fate of these 20 or so prisoners, which is exactly what Fatmir Limaj seems to suggest. Third, Shukri Buja. Buja testified that he later saw the released prisoners and he immediately tried, although unsuccessfully, to contact Klecka. He later spoke about the incident. Buja also testified -- excuse me, said in his OTP interview that Klecka dealt with arrested persons. And finally, Your Honours, it is certainly not accepted by the Prosecution that Fatmir Limaj could not have been where L-96 saw him because of health reasons. Nothing about Limaj's claimed illness would have prevented him from being where L-94 saw him. On Limaj's own testimony he spent the 26th of 1998 going from village to village to village in the area, not far from where L-96 saw him. Your Honour, could you give me an indication of when you'd like me to take the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: About another 10 to 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll proceed. At this point, it may be appropriate to say a few words about modes of liability. Now, the evidence supporting the various modes of liability and how they relate to the various crimes is addressed in some detail in our final brief, and I won't repeat that effort here. Nevertheless, I'd like to make a couple of points very briefly. We submit that the starting point in this case is joint criminal enterprise. As addressed by Mr. Whiting, each of the accused had an important role in the functioning and operation of the Lapusnik camp. Now, whether the Trial Chamber's inclined to view this case of JCE 2 or a system of ill-treatment or an ordinary common criminal plan under JCE 1, it is plain that the camp was an organised system for the unlawful detention, mistreatment, torture, and murder of Serb and Albanian civilians. By intentionally participating in that joint criminal enterprise and furthering it, all three accused are responsible, as alleged in the indictment. There was also substantial evidence specifically tying the accused to various criminal acts. That, too, is set forth in the final brief. Just to summarise, in many cases the evidence establishes the direct personal participation of Haradin Bala and Isak Musliu in serious violent crime at the camp. The evidence as a whole also strongly supports the charges that Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu planned, ordered, and instigated many of the crimes charged in the indictment. In addition to the evidence of their command positions, the evidence shows that they were both personally present at the camp, that Isak Musliu at least personally participated in violence, and that Fatmir Limaj personally witnessed some of those incidents. Yet they took no action to stop the openly criminal behaviour at the Lapusnik prison camp. This evidence, Your Honours, is important for intent as well as notice. And in fact, we submit that in addition to their criminal failure to prevent or punish under Article 7(3) both Limaj and Musliu by their wilful inaction and by their own example instigated and aided and abetted the the crimes at the camp. I'll now address two specific points with regard to Isak Musliu, both arising from the Defence final brief. The first one, although it's not particularly clear, the Defence appear to suggest at paragraph 901 of their final brief that Musliu was not charged with the murders in Annex I. Certainly they're not addressed in the Musliu section of the brief. It is clear from the indictment, however, that Musliu is indeed charged with all of the murders in Counts 7 and 8. True, he was not charged with "personally participating in or aiding and abetting" the Annex I murders, but that refers to just two of the applicable modes of liability. As is clear from paragraph 28 and Counts 7 and 8 of the indictment as a whole, Musliu is charged with planning, ordering, and instigating those murders as well as with participation in JCE and superior responsibility under Article 7(3). Now, I don't know if I need to belabour this point, but I would note that Musliu's suggested reading of those counts would leave Limaj completely uncharged with any of the murders in Counts 7 and 8. That is obviously unreconcilable with paragraph 28 and the language of the counts themselves. Finally on this issue, I note that in paragraph 30 of Musliu's pre-trial brief he denied responsibility for the deaths of all 14 men named in connection with Counts 7 and 8. He thus knew from early in these proceedings that he was and is charged with both the Annex I and Annex II murders. Second, throughout his section of the Defence final brief, Musliu seeks to minimise the evidence against him by distinguishing between evidence against Isak Musliu and evidence against Qerqiz. This is a false distinction, of course. Musliu has never denied using the pseudonym Qerqiz, and there has been no suggestion during trial of any other Qerqizes in the camp or in Lapusnik more generally, as far as I am aware. The Prosecution submits that there are three broad categories of evidence that can and should be considered in determining Musliu's responsibility. First, that evidence which identifies him by name or from a photograph as Isak Musliu; two, or second, that evidence which refers to Qerqiz; and third, that evidence which, as is set out in our final brief, describes a person who very closely matches the description of Isak Musliu, both in terms of his physical characteristics and also other identifying information such as his karate experience. We submit that all of this evidence should be considered by the Trial Chamber and accorded whatever weight is deemed appropriate, but it should be considered in determining his role in the JCE and his responsibility under Articles 7(1) and 7(3). Your Honours, this is probably an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First I'd like to make one small correction to the record. It's at page 39 of the LiveNote transcript. I referred to Prosecution Exhibit 129 as P245 tab 2, but in fact it's tab 3. So it's a minor point but I just wanted to clarify that. Your Honours, in the time that's remaining for me I'd like to address three additional arguments made in the Defence final brief. The first is a minor legal issue. The Defence attack us for arresting in our opening that an accused could be found to aid and abet a JCE. However, as they essentially concede, the Appeals Chamber decision which finally clarified the relationship between participation in a JCE and aiding and abetting and distinguished between those two things, that decision came down after this trial started. The argument is not pursued in our final brief, just to be clear on that. The second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We take it you do not question, then, the outcome, as reflected in the Appeals Chamber decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The second issue is more significant. The Defence suggest in their final brief that several Prosecution witnesses were kidnapped for personal reasons, essentially unconnected with the armed conflict. My first point in response would be that the Appeals Chamber in Tadic made quite clear that the commission of a crime for "purely personal motives" does not exclude that crime from the jurisdiction of this Tribunal so long as the jurisdictional requirements are met. And you can find that discussion at paragraphs 248 to 252 of the Tadic Appeals judgement. Second, the evidence is clear in this case that the crimes committed against these individuals were closely connected to the conflict regardless of the personal motives of the actual kidnappers. The evidence demonstrates that the witnesses at issue were kidnapped by members of the KLA, they were then taken to KLA headquarters en route to the camp, they were transferred to a KLA camp in Lapusnik, and there they were interrogated about Serb spies in their villages and other collaboration topics. Moreover, Ramadan Behluli testified in this courtroom that he considered two of them to be collaborators. The connection to the affirmed conflict and particularly the KLA's policy on collaborators could hardly be stronger. A closely related argument by the Defence suggests that these witnesses were kidnapped by rogue elements. However, there's no question that the kidnappers were members of the KLA, and it hardly seems plausible, in our submission, that rogue elements would process the victims through local KLA headquarters before transferring them to a centralised KLA facility housing prisoners from all over the region. It simply defies reason. Turning then to my last issue. The Defence argue in their final brief at several places that collaborators targeted by the KLA were people actively involved with the Serbian authorities, thus apparently suggesting that the prisoners in the Lapusnik camp were actually collaborators. None of the Albanian victims who testified in this case were cross-examined about whether they were actually collaborators, with the possible exception, I guess, of some suggestions made to Witness L-96. So we're left somewhat uncertain about just what the Defence position is. But in any event, as addressed by Mr. Whiting earlier, the evidence was overwhelming that in reality charges of collaboration were based on a much broader range of activities which included ordinary business and social contacts with Serbs. This comes through in a number of ways in the evidence, including but not limited to the communiques, the testimony of Jakup Krasniqi and Ramadan Behluli; the evidence about Ramiz Hoxha and Selman Binici; the detention of Witness L-07; the interrogation of victims at Lapusnik -- for example, one was asked why he had sold wood to Serbs; also from the testimony of Susanne Ringaard-Pedersen; the notes concerning Witness L-96 which were found in Lapusnik which are viewed at tab 5 to Prosecution Exhibit 245; and also by the notes found in Fatmir Limaj's apartment which refer to murder victim Lutfi Xhemshiti, and those are in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit P30. Furthermore, Your Honours, it is undisputed that there were absolutely no KLA procedures for determining who was in fact a collaborator or for reviewing any such determination. Indeed, one of the things that comes across from this case is the fundamental importance of procedural safeguards, particularly in connection with detention facilities. There was no such thing as due process in the Lapusnik prison camp. I hasten to add, however, that this entire issue of process and "actual collaborators or real collaborators" is relevant only to the charges of imprisonment. I do not understand the Defence to argue that the other crimes alleged in the indictment from inhumane conditions through to torture, beatings, and extra judicial murder could ever be justified against any prisoners, regardless of the suspicions or charges against them. Your Honours, those are the issues that I planned to address. In a moment, Mr. Nicholls will address some issues relating to armed conflict and widespread and systematic attack under Articles 3 and 5. But let me say in conclusion: As in any criminal case, the Prosecution bears the burden of proving these charges beyond reasonable doubt. We accept that burden and we have satisfied it and we would ask the Trial Chamber to find the accused guilty as charged. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. When it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As Mr. Black said, I'm going to briefly address the topics of armed conflict and some of the evidence relating to the widespread or systematic attack. First, armed conflict. The law is quite clear in this regard, and I will spend just a little time discussing the legal standards in this case. The test which is laid out well in the Milosevic Rule 98 bis decision from last year is as follows, this is at paragraph 16 to 17: "The test for an armed conflict consistently applied within this Tribunal was set forth in the Tadic jurisdiction decision: An armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between states or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a state." The Milosevic Chamber concluded that this test there calls for an examination: 1, of the organisation of the parties to the conflict; and 2, the intensity of the conflict. The Milosevic Trial Chamber explained the purpose of this test as follows: "The main purpose of the Tadic test is to distinguish an armed conflict from banditry, unorganised and short-lived insurrections, or terrorist activities, all of which are not subject to international law." That is the extent of the inquiry necessary to establish an armed conflict for purposes of Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute. It's not necessary for Your Honours to determine whether the conflict was internal or international in character. Now, this Trial Chamber recognised that in the Strugar judgement at paragraph 216, writing that Article 3 of the Statute is applicable regardless of the nature of the conflict, international or internal. And of course the same is true of Article 5, as provided for in the text of the article. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In a moment I'm going to outline some of the evidence presented at trial which proves that the Prosecution has met its burden, satisfying both prongs of the Tadic test. The evidence in this case has shown that the armed conflict in Kosovo during the indictment period was of a scale far above banditry, unorganised and short-lived insurrections or terrorist activities. First, though, I'll address some of the legal arguments put forth by the Defence in their brief regarding armed conflict. It's clear from the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that Article 3 of the Statute covers violations of Common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions, and Common Article 3 of course being applicable to internal armed conflicts. In Strugar, the Chamber held that it's well established at Article 3 of the Statute, covers violations of Common Article 3. And that's at paragraph 219. In paragraph 205 of their brief, the Defence purport to address the intent of the drafters of Common Article 3 regarding its application by reference to the ICRC commentary to Common Article 3, and the Defence then in the next paragraph list the helpful criteria contained in the commentary. Now, I'm not going to read through the commentary and the criteria which are set forth in the brief and which I'm sure Your Honours are well aware of. But I note that the Defence have omitted from their joint brief the crystal-clear statement in the commentary regarding the ICRC's view of the nature of the criteria and the application of Common Article 3. And I'll briefly discuss that view because as the Defence have correctly suggested, the commentary is an indicator of the intent of the drafters of Common Article 3. The ICRC's characterisation of the criteria and the application of Common Article 3 is as follows -- before listing the criteria, the commentary states: "...these different conditions, although in no way obligatory, constitute convenient criteria," and then they continue to list them. After listing these several criteria the commentary states: "The above criteria are useful as a means of distinguishing a genuine armed conflict from a mere act of banditry or an unorganised and short-lived insurrection. Does this mean that Article 3 is not applicable in cases where armed strife breaks out in a country but does not fulfil any of the above conditions which are not obligatory and which are only mentioned as an indication? We do not subscribe to this view. We think, on the contrary, that Article 3 should be applied as widely as possible. It's plain, therefore, that the helpful criteria are not requirements, they're not elements which must be established before the protections and the obligations of Article 3 attached to an internal armed conflict, and that this was the intent of the drafters. Let me just briefly quote what the Milosevic Chamber held regarding this very issue, that's at paragraph 19 of the same decision. In this regard the Trial Chamber observes that the ICRC's commentary is nothing more than what it purports to be, i.e., a commentary, and only has persuasive value. The ICRC commentary sets out a more extensive list of criteria than the Tadic test, which may be considered when determining whether an armed conflict exists. But the ICRC itself states that these different conditions, although in no way obligatory, constitute convenient criteria. As such, the ICRC criteria are neither definitive nor exhaustive and Common Article 3 should apply as widely as possible. Nevertheless, Your Honours, I believe the evidence shows, though not obligatory, definitive, or exhaustive, that these criteria have been met in this case. Additional Protocol II. The Defence spends some part of their brief discussing the application of Additional Protocol II to the 1949 Geneva Conventions to this case. Again, the Milosevic 98 bis decision makes clear that the only test applied in this Tribunal is the Tadic test and that there is absolutely no burden on the Prosecution to satisfy the requirements of Additional Protocol II. As an example, in paragraph 36 of the Milosevic decision the Chamber held that the ability of the KLA to exercise and maintain control over a part of the territory of Kosovo is not a requirement for the existence of an armed conflict. Again, Your Honours, although it's not required, the evidence shows that these -- that the criteria of Additional Protocol II have in fact been met in this case. Finally, Your Honours, the Defence argues beginning at paragraph 67 -- paragraph 184, page 67 of their brief, that "the present case is covered by Additional Protocol I." They refer there to the Protocol Additional to the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and relating to the protection of victims of international armed conflicts. I only say, Your Honours, this is a bit of an odd argument for the Defence to make, for Additional Protocol 1 applies to armed conflicts. If it applies to this case, it applies to an armed conflict in this case. I said some moments ago, it's absolutely immaterial whether that armed conflict is internal or international. The jurisdictional element of armed conflict for purposes of our Statute is satisfied in either case. I would also draw your attention to the findings of Peter Bouckaert and the other lawyers of Human Rights Watch and Susan Ringaard Pedersen and the OSCE-KVM, that in fact the conflict in Kosovo was an internal armed conflict, subject to Common Article 3 and the Additional Protocol II. Human Rights Watch found that a state of internal armed conflict existed in Kosovo from 28 February 1998. And I note, Your Honours, the Defence brief is therefore inaccurate at paragraph 345 where the last sentence asserts that there is "no indication" that international observers on the ground in Kosovo during the indictment period viewed the conflict as rising to the level of an armed conflict. That assertion is false. In addition, Mr. Bouckaert stressed in his testimony here during cross-examination that Human Rights Watch sought to implement international humanitarian law within its established boundaries, not to push those boundaries, for fear that doing so would undermine or dilute the protections of international humanitarian law. And that's at transcript reference 5546. Lastly on this issue, it should be borne in mind that the KLA frequently pledged that it respected and would abide by international law in an effort to garner support from the international community. One example: KLA spokesman Jakup Krasniqi in his testimony here authenticated P142, which is an official KLA communique of 29 April 1998. That communique states: "We are in a state of war... the KLA recognises and respects the international treaties of the United Nations and the conventions on war. We appeal to the international decision-making centres, the European Union, and especially the USA, to increase pressure on our occupiers in the name of peace and to support the just war of our nation." Further, Krasniqi authenticated as genuine in Exhibit P48, an interview he gave on the 11th and 12th of July 1998 in which he stated: "The KLA recognises the Geneva Convention and the conventions governing the conduct of war." Testifying about this interview, Mr. Krasniqi stated that in fact at this time, mid-July, the KLA had received written materials regarding the Geneva Conventions. The question was: "Q. First of all, I want to ask you about what you saw in this answer about the 'internal rules for our operations,' which 'clearly lay down that the UCK recognises the Geneva Conventions and the conventions governing the conduct of war.' Were those rules written down at this time? Did you have the written rules that you're referring to here?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRASNIQI'S ANSWER
utterances.text: "A. Yes. The International Red Cross had sent us some concrete documents which the KLA should respect these Conventions. It was a document that we circulated at this time; that's why we say here that the KLA has not dealt with civilians." Finally, Fatmir Limaj testified that he was present with Jakup Krasniqi during a meeting with Jan Kickert on 30th of July in Klecka, at which time Krasniqi prejudiced that the KLA would respect its responsibilities under international law. And Limaj also testified that in July he personally possessed written instructions from the ICRC concerning the treatment of prisoners. That's at transcript 6563 to 64. Looking now at the facts, at the evidence, of armed conflict in this case. The evidence proves beyond reasonable doubt that during the indictment period the organisation of the parties to the conflict - Serbian forces on the one hand and the KLA - and the intensity of the conflict were well both above of a scale of that necessary to distinguish an armed conflict in Kosovo from banditry, unorganised and short-lived insurrections, or terrorist activities. I'll briefly look at both prongs of the test. We don't dispute that the KLA was not as organised and developed at the VJ in its organisational structure. And there is no requirement in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal requiring a level of organisation equivalent to that of a professional army. Even under the higher standards set forth in Additional Protocol II, there is no requirement of a hierarchical command equivalent to that of a professional army. In interpreting Additional Protocol II the ICTR in the Musema case held that: "Furthermore, the armed forces opposing the government must be under responsible command. This requirement implies some degree of organisation within the armed groups or dissident armed forces, but this does not necessarily mean that there is a hierarchical system of military command similar to that of regular armed forces." That's at paragraph 257. And indeed, it is likely that in virtually all internal armed conflicts, those subject to Common Article 3, that the rebels or insurgents are going to be less organised and less well armed in comparison to the regular armed forces. And these are just the conflicts that Common Article 3 is intended to apply to. And as well here today, Mr. Whiting has covered the command exercised by Fatmir Limaj during the indictment period. I will not repeat those facts, other than to say that the evidence proves and has been laid out that Mr. Fatmir Limaj was an effective commander of soldiers organised into units. He commanded an organised armed group. That command is of course only a part of the overall KLA forces that were organised in the summer of 1998. For example, Sylejman Selimi, when he testified here spoke about how he was appointed commander of the Drenica zone by the General Staff at the end of May 1998. The Drenica zone, which is perhaps, the evidence has been, the most advanced zone, extended south to the Pristina-Peja highway and Lapusnik. Selimi testified that immediately upon taking command he began consolidating the existing units into brigades and he appointed commanders. On the other side of the Pristina-Peja highway the soldiers of the Celiku 3 were organised in a system, as we've heard today again, of five fighting positions, each of which had a commander for that position. Ruzhdi Karpuzi who had been assigned to position 1 of Celiku 3, as Mr. Black said authenticated the Celiku 3 position 1 logbook that was found in Lapusnik at the end of July. He explained that that book is a record of the round-the-clock, 24-hour-a-day surveillance of the highway and the checkpoints. So there we have continuous surveillance by soldiers assigned to shifts under the position commander, and keeping records of all movements on the terrain. Selimi also confirmed that units on either side of the Pristina-Peja highway communicated with each other as necessary regarding the highway, sometimes by radio or otherwise if they were close, and that unit commanders would order that permits were issued to soldiers in order to allow them to cross the highway when necessary. And of course, KLA travel permits also found in Lapusnik in July 1998 have been introduced into evidence. That's at P245, tab 8. Selimi also admitted during his testimony, somewhat reluctantly, that KLA commanders had the disciplinary power to take the weapons away from KLA soldiers for misconduct, and to eject them from their units. Although, as the Defence state in their brief at paragraph 306, Selimi claimed that disciplining his subordinates was not necessary because all the soldiers followed his orders. Another issue covered in the trial is the procurement of weapons by the KLA. Control of the Pristina-Peja highway was important to the KLA. According to Selimi, the strategy of the KLA was to keep control of this highway as a corridor for arms and weapons from Albania as well as to prevent incursions along the Pristina-Peja highway by Serb forces. Another witness with first hand knowledge, L-95, in the beginning of his testimony described the executions of missions into Albania for the purposes of obtaining arms for the KLA and bringing them back to his headquarters. That's at transcript reference 4185 to 4192. Again, demonstrating the ability of the KLA to organise the procurement and distribution of arms. John Crosland also testified from his experience on the ground about the ability of the KLA as early as March 1998 to organise the importation of weapons. He was commenting at one point on the contents of a United Kingdom diplomatic telegram which concerned combat on the 24th of March, 1998, in Decane municipality, which is on the western border of Kosovo. Crosland stated: "This was just an indication that the conflict, having spread from the area of the Drenica just to the west of Pristina, was now coming over to the western side, which was not -- was nothing unusual to us because it was clear from an early stage that reinforcements and resupplies were coming in over the Albanian border, what I would call the corridor, through to Decani and then on into Klina and then on into the Drenica to supply men in the eastern area with the equipment to continue the conflict against the Serbian security forces." Crosland also testified in addition to bringing in arms and men that the soldiers brought in through this corridor had been trained for combat in Albanian camps. Limaj himself recounted a conversation he had in June 1998 with Jakup Krasniqi, who told him that almost the entire General Staff had engaged in procuring weapons because the question of weapons was the number one question. So they were all interested in getting as much weapons as possible and arming people who wanted to get armed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If I could come back just for a moment to Witness L-95. He also testified about the organisation of the KLA headquarters and the prison facilities that he was familiar with in another area of Kosovo. I'm not going to talk in detail about that testimony, which is found at 4247 to 4277. However, I suggest to Your Honours that the testimony of this witness provides evidence of very similar command and control structures, headquarters, and prison facilities as those which are the subject of this indictment. Additionally, Your Honours, I'd ask you perhaps to look carefully at the testimony of L-95 found at pages 4203 to 4244 regarding how he and his unit were ordered to go and assist another unit which was in danger of attack and the subsequent events and meetings that he observed. The General Staff. The Defence in paragraph 276, this is an on-and-off issue, question whether there was actually a KLA General Staff. It's an incredible claim, especially as in paragraph 281 they cite to General Staff member Rexhaj Selimi's testimony that during the indictment period the General Staff would move around for security reasons. That does not mean, as suggested by the Defence, that there was no communication with the General Staff by commanders. Selimi again testified that in May -- that at the end of May the General Staff represented in person by Rexhaj Selimi, appointed him commander of Drenica. The spokesman for the KLA and member of the General Staff, Jakup Krasniqi, testified in this trial that the General Staff had an armed wing and a political wing and that he had always been a member of the political wing. Krasniqi at page 3415 of the transcript told us how the commanders in different zones had a duty to inform the General Staff about events in their zones. Fatmir Limaj testified how in June he was heartened to meet several professional military officers who had joined the KLA and, in his words: "Via the General Staff they were observing the terrain. And if I say, they were in a way surveying the terrain and every unit." Limaj continued to explain how one of these soldiers, Agim Qelaj, took three or four of Limaj's soldiers to join soldiers that Qelaj had selected from other units in order to bring them together into a special intervention unit. Limaj testified that Qelaj trained and prepared these soldiers. This testimony, the meeting of these officers with Limaj, is corroborated by Defence witness Byslym Zyrapi. Further, again, according to Limaj in his testimony here, during the fighting in Orahovac in July, the General Staff assigned Agim Qelaj as operations manager for Orahovac during the fighting. The evidence, then, for the General Staff is that it had an armed wing; commanders reported to the General Staff; the General Staff appointed Selimi to his position of the Drenica commander; the General Staff engaged in procuring weapons for the troops; the General Staff arranged for professional military officers to survey the terrain and the units; and that this led to the formation and training of at least one intervention unit, which included soldiers from Limaj's command. The General Staff was not, as claimed by Robert Churcher and the Defence in their brief at paragraph 280, a mythical concept. And this incorrect statement by Churcher, I would suggest, is just one of several reasons why his testimony and report should be viewed with caution. If I can quickly sum up. During the period covered by our indictment, the KLA constituted an organised armed group for the purposes of the Tadic test. The evidence demonstrates that the KLA was organised in a fighting system of units and fighting positions, and that every position had a commander. There were KLA headquarters and different zones of operation. Units assisted other units when necessary. There has been quite a lot of testimony about that, as well as L-95's testimony that his unit was sent to do so by his commander. There is evidence that soldiers were hand-picked to form a special unit. At the fighting positions, at that level, things were organised into shifts around the clock in order to monitor the terrain for troop movements and logbooks were kept in order to record which soldiers were on duty and what activity it observed from their positions. And I've covered just now the activities of the General Staff in military matters. Additionally, records were kept of the personal details of soldiers and of the weapons issued to them; this was one of Ruzhdi Karpuzi's duties in Lapusnik. Commanders had the power to discipline soldiers by removing their weapons and ejecting them from the KLA. There were medical facilities set up for KLA fighters, and of course there were detention facilities built, including the one in Lapusnik. There is also the evidence of oath ceremonies and of written regulations. Both Limaj and Ramiz Qeriqi received these written regulations, this code. It's in evidence as Exhibit P156. Qeriqi testified that he believed it came from the General Staff and that he and Shukri Buja received it around June 1998. He wasn't sure of the date exactly, but in any event he remembered for sure that it was before the July offensive. Qeriqi stated that it was distributed to the soldiers to read. And Limaj here testified that he received these regulations which he referred to as "a rule book" and that he received it around the 22nd or 23rd of June and read it. The KLA was an organised armed group under the first prong of the Tadic test. The second prong, the intensity of the conflict. I think the evidence here is very clear that the prolonged and intense nature of the armed violence in Kosovo from May through July 1998 was of a scale far, far above acts of banditry, short-lived or unorganised insurrections or terrorist activities. I'll focus on some of the factors the Milosevic Chamber looked to in determining that an armed conflict existed in Kosovo. These are the length or protracted nature of the conflict, the spread of clashes over the territory, the increase in governmental forces, and the weaponry used by both sides. And in our case as well there's been a lot of testimony about the increasing KLA forces and the explosive growth in KLA membership after February/March 1998. In addition, the Milosevic Chamber did not accept that there was any requirement that the KLA be organised under a civil authority, nor that it exercise control over territory. However, the Chamber found that in any case, both of those non-essential criteria had been met. As far as the protracted nature of the conflict, there was armed conflict -- there was attacks by the KLA before May 1998, before the indictment period. In his testimony before you, Jakup Krasniqi confirmed operations conducted by the KLA in August and November 1997, which included killing so-called collaborators and members of the MUP. Rexhep Selimi, Defence witness, testified to taking part, in his words, a synchronised KLA attack against 12 MUP stations on 11 November 1997 and fighting Serb forces armed with a helicopter, armoured vehicles, and tanks near Acareve on 26 of November, 1997. Jumping now to the period after 26th of July and the fall of Lapusnik. The armed conflict in Kosovo continued with great intensity, John Crosland testified based on his personal observations of numerous clashes between the KLA and Serbian forces from the end of July through November 1998. At the end of July, he talked about in his testimony a 30th of July daily report from the Pec military department describing strong and fierce resistance by the KLA to mopping-up operations being conducted by the MUP together with the VJ in the area of Iglarevo, Kijevo, and Junik. And Crosland testified that the fighting unit had been going on for three months prior to the combat operation referred to on the 30th of July report. He also testified about incidents of armed conflict in August, September, and November and explained that his testimony concerning the figure of 163 UCK attacks between 13 October and 20th November contained in a 23 November situation report from the British embassy referred to KLA attacks of different degrees of severity. That report is Prosecution Exhibit 92 at tab 42. The spread of clashes over the territory. There has been much discussion about that and that occurred primarily during the indictment period. There has been a great deal of evidence accelerated the spread of violent confrontations between the KLA and Serb forces across much of Kosovo during the summer of 1998. By the end of March it was clear that the armed conflict was spreading out of Drenica. John Crosland, referring to the UK diplomatic telegram I talked about earlier from the 24th of March, 1998, testified that at that time the conflict was spreading west towards the Albanian border along the weapons corridor. According to Crosland, at the end of May there was also heavy fighting continuing in Decani and Drenica, and as many witnesses have testified to there was heavy fighting in Lapusnik at the end of May. Also at the end of May, John Crosland testified that now the conflict began to spread east from Drenica, in the other direction. Your Honours also have in evidence numerous contemporaneous documents from the Pristina Corps, the VJ, ECMM, KLA communiques that are also useful in establishing the spread of armed violence over Kosovo. These are discussed in Philip Coo's report and contained in the annexes to that report. And I will discuss just a few of them. The 13th of May report to the 3rd Army of Command by Major General Pavkovic, commander of the entire Pristina core, makes clear that in his assessment the conflict zone was spreading rapidly. And that's Exhibit P92 at tab 17. That report is corroborated completely by ECMM documentation and even KLA communiques, specifically communique number 47 from the same time period, 12th of May, which is entitled: "Our army has broken the enemy's attacks and is extending the liberated areas." This communique boasts of the KLA's success and its assessment of the spread of combat operations matches that made by General Pavkovic. During this same period, ECMM monitors on the ground in Kosovo reported a dramatic intensification of KLA operations. Same time period, 15th of May weekly assessment report described the escalation of the armed conflict as follows: "Mobile team Belgrade's observations on the ground hint that another crucial corner has been turned in Kosovo. The UCK until a few weeks ago still a mystery with its structure, leadership, tactics, and funding sources and political connections, widely unknown, has come to life and into focus of public attention. From a more defensive posture during the February and March clashes, the UCK has now taken the initiative and is carrying the war to the Serbian security forces. An example of the change in their tactics has been the closure of the Pristina-Pec road, the main supply route for the Serbian security forces, for more than four days." And that's contained, I'm reminded to tell you by Mr. Younis, in Philip Coo's report that's P230. It's in Annex D. On 30 June 1998 the New York Times reported on the escalation of the conflict and fighting between Serbian forces and the KLA in Lapusnik and Belacevac in an article entitled "Serb forces open a major assault on Kosovo rebels." The article states: "'The Serbs believe this is the final offensive,' a Western military observer said. 'But this is the third attempt since March by the Serbian security forces to wipe out the rebels. Each attempt has brought only an escalation of the fighting. So will this one.'" That's P233. The assessment by that anonymous observer proved to be correct. Philip Coo testified that the facts asserted in that New York Times article were corroborated by the VJ and ECMM documentation that he reviewed when preparing his report. In addition to the various battles in Lapusnik, which there has been much testimony about, witnesses have testified to their participation in or observation of clashes in other places from May through July. These included Kroimire, Carraleve, Zborce, Petrastica, Djakovica, Ponosevac, Junik, Grabanica, Ratkoc, Rahovec, and Luznica. And the cites for those armed clashes are in paragraph 248 of our brief. There has also been a lot of testimony, and I won't go over it, about the Serbian offensive at the end of July 1998 when the VJ and MUP launched a massive assault against KLA-held positions and territory throughout Kosovo. The entire PrK was involved in the July offensive in addition of course to specialised MUP units trained for armed combat. The evidence fully supports the statement of military expert Coo that from May 1998 Serb forces were engaged in armed clashes with the KLA on a sustained basis over a large part of Kosovo. The assertion of the Defence in paragraph 255 of their brief that "there were very few instances of fighting in the whole of Kosovo up to the end of July 1998" is just not true. The response of Serbian forces to the escalation of the conflict. I'll cover that very quickly. As Mr. Coo testified, the entire PrK was put on full combat alert. Additionally, the forces of the PrK were increased and its structure altered as the intensity of the conflict increased. During the indictment period Belgrade supplemented the brigades of the PrK with troops from the Belgrade-based 72nd Special Forces Brigade and the 63rd Parachute Brigade, in addition to establishing forward command posts for the Pristina corps as well as for the 3rd Army in Kosovo. Another Milosevic criteria. The weapons used by the parties. Very clearly, the weapons used by both sides in this conflict were of the type typically used in war, as opposed to police actions or terrorist actions, although clearly, the Serbian forces had vastly superior weaponry at their disposal. The VJ and MUP combat units were armed with tanks, armoured personnel carriers, helicopters, artillery, anti-aircraft artillery systems, and all of these heavy weapons systems, except for helicopters as far as I can tell, were used against the KLA positions in Lapusnik. The KLA, we've heard, was armed with automatic rifles, sniper rifles, heavy recoilless rifles or heavy machine-guns, rocket-propelled grenades or RPGs, mortars, as well as with hunting rifles and revolvers and home-made weapons. Although it's not a requirement for the Tadic test, I'll briefly address control of the territory by the KLA. As the armed conflict intensified and spread, the KLA successfully seized control of significant area of the territory in Kosovo. In the period before the July offensive, the VJ and international observers agreed with -- that the KLA were in control of an estimated 30 to 40 per cent of Kosovo. The evidence shows that the KLA's successes were due to planning and were the product of a strategy of linking KLA-held areas to expand their territory Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and, most importantly, to protect the flow of weapons and troops which ran from Albania to Drenica. According to Crosland, by late April 1998 the VJ was "genuinely afraid of losing control of significant parts of Kosovo." The VJ report of the 13th of May that I referred to earlier, General Pavkovic's report to the 3rd Army, estimated that 30 per cent of Kosovo was in control of the KLA, including the strategically important Pristina-Peja road. Peter Bouckaert testified here and Human Rights Watch found at the time that from April through mid-July the KLA controlled about 40 per cent of Kosovo. John Crosland again in his testimony here agreed that as of 23rd of June the KLA controlled 35 per cent of Kosovo but could mount attacks in 65 per cent of Kosovo. Crosland explained that control of territory was fluid during the war, as one side would move in, the other would withdraw and vice versa. He called it back-filling the territory. However, he confirmed that the figure of 35 per cent was accurate. Now, this inherently fluid nature of the control of territory during internal armed conflicts is specifically recognised in the commentary to Additional Protocol Ii. I'll read a bit of the paragraph which is the commentary to paragraph 1 of Article 1 of that protocol. "In many conflicts there is a considerable movement in the theatre of hostilities. It often happens that territorial control changes hands rapidly. Sometimes domination of a territory will be relative, for example when urban centres remain in government hands while rural centres escape their authority. In practical terms, if the insurgent armed groups are organised in accordance with the requirements of the protocol, the extent of the territory they can claim to control will be that which escapes the control of the government armed forces. However, there must be some degree of stability in the control of even a modest area of land for them to be capable of effectively applying the rules of the protocol." That degree of stability has been proven in this case: The KLA controlled a large area of territory. They controlled roads and supply lines. They set up checkpoints. They built fortified bunkers and trenches along the front lines. They established clinics, cooking facilities, places to store records, warehouses, detention facilities. And of course the KLA successfully held Lapusnik for three months against multiple assaults from the Serb forces. In June, ECMM reported that by active operations and the arming of the population in and around Malisevo, the KLA was trying to take control of central Kosovo and that the so-called liberated area was growing. According to a 16th of June ECMM report, the report notes that Malisevo was central to this new liberated territory and these reports were also in Annex D of P230. On 22nd June, the ECMM reported that the KLA had made impressive gains in its control of the territory and infrastructure. These ECMM assessments are supported by the testimony of Defence witness Byslym Zyrapi, the former VJ and Bosnian army colonel. Zyrapi here testified that Malisevo was the centre of the free zone. And John Crosland testified that this had begun quite early, that already in April 1998 the KLA's strategy was to link Drenica and Decani, two areas where the Serbs have the least control. When you look at all that evidence, those operations, that control of the territory, the evidence shows the Defence is simply wrong when it characterises the conflict as a series of shoot-and-run style operations, as it does in paragraph 203. The evidence has established both prongs necessary for the Tadic test. I'll try to talk very quickly about some of the evidence now of attacks on civilians. During the indictment period the KLA conducted attacks over a wide area of Kosovo against Serb civilians as well as Albanians loosely and arbitrarily labelled as collaborators. Mr. Whiting and Mr. Black have already spoken quite a bit about this issue, and I'll try not to repeat what they said. But confronted with this situation, specifically in reference to the kidnapping of some of the victims in this case, Ivan and Vojko Bakrac, Djordje Cuk, Stamen Genov, on the 29th of June, ECMM reported that the ICRC and UNHCR were increasingly concerned with the KLA strategy of kidnapping. Mr. Black has discussed the crimes committed against victims in this case. Those crimes represent only a fraction of the attacks on civilians by the KLA in 1998. These attacks were not random. They weren't committed by rogue elements. A very early example is the hand grenade attack carried out by Defence witness and General Staff member Rexhep Selimi, who admitted to throwing a hand grenade he said near, not at, a hostel for Serb refugees in Pristina in 1996. Although he claimed that this attack was only meant to sent Serb colonisers, in his view, a message and claimed that they should thank him for letting them know that a war was coming. Another example. During the indictment period, John Crosland testified that the KLA regularly conducted attacks to kidnap Serb civilians in the Klina region. Crosland testified that areas in the vicinity of a KLA headquarters were particularly hazardous for civilians, including Carraleve. Crosland said, "As regards Carraleve, it was a UCK -- a KLA headquarters and therefore people going through that area were liable to be hijacked and used for KLA activity." Crosland was also familiar with KLA attacks on the Serb civilian population in the Obiliq municipality in the Llap zone. He commented on a VJ report of the 18th of June which reported the abduction of five Serbs from an area near the Belacevac mine. That's Exhibit P92 at tab 26. Crosland testified that the mine was in an area with a mainly Serb population, which was attacked out of Drenica by the KLA. The danger from the KLA to the Serb civilian population in Belacevac was such that the civilian population was forced to make a choice between protecting themselves on their own against KLA attacks or abandoning their homes. Crosland explained that the efforts of the Serb population of Belacevac represented a classic case of Serbs arming to defend their villages in order to avoid being forced to leave their homes. This testimony from John Crosland -- should I stop now or go for another two minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As you prefer. You have, at the most, two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll make one more point, Your Honours, and that's just this: That this testimony of Crosland is corroborated by the findings of Human Rights Watch and the OSCE. Human Rights Watch found that KLA operations - some KLA operations, not all - were apparently intended to drive ethnic Serbs out of their villages and that there were credible reports of ethnic Serbs being forced to leave the villages of Jelovac, Kijevo, Leocina, Gorni Ratis, Maznik, Dasinovac, Veliki Djurdjevak, Mlecane, Dubrava, Boksic, and Lugodjija. And because I've mispronounced some of those, I'll tell you the reference is Exhibit P212 at tab 5 at K0364865. Finally, OSCE-KVM in their report "as Seen As Told," which is in evidence as P150, concluded that one of the main threats to the Serb community at this time was the UCK. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. We'll hear the balance of your submissions in the course of tomorrow afternoon and Mr. Whiting will finish. And it would seem we would be able to move on to the Defence in the course of the day. Thank you. We'll adjourn now until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of August, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
